{"query": "WITH os AS (
    SELECT patient_unique_id,
        maxIf(toFloat64OrNull(attribute_value), attribute_name = 'OS_MONTHS') AS os_months,
        maxIf(attribute_value, attribute_name = 'OS_STATUS') AS os_status

    countIf(startsWith(os_status, '1')) AS n_events_deceased,

    round(min(os_months), 2) AS min_followup_months,

question.question: Which KRAS mutations are most common in colorectal cancer?

reply.answer:
The most common KRAS mutations in colorectal cancer, in the TCGA PanCancer Atlas colorectal study (COADREAD, 534 samples profiled for KRAS), are at codons 12 and 13:

| Rank | KRAS variant | Samples with variant | % of profiled samples |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | G12D | 58 | 10.9% |
| 2 | G12V | 49 | 9.2% |
| 3 | G13D | 37 | 6.9% |
| 4 | A146T | 16 | 3.0% |
| 5 | G12C | 15 | 2.8% |
| 6 | G12A | 10 | 1.9% |
| 7 | G12S | 8 | 1.5% |

Counts are samples, not patients. Only the top 15 variants were retrieved; the rest each occur in 4 or fewer samples. The variants shown are all missense changes. I have not checked whether they are driver or oncogenic annotations, since this study has no driver annotation in the database.

This reflects one study, so it may not generalize to all colorectal cancers. Other colorectal studies in the database could show different distributions, and I did not query them.

Study page: [Colorectal Adenocarcinoma (TCGA, PanCancer Atlas)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=coadread_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018)

I could not generate a direct link to the KRAS mutations view because the link-generation service is currently unavailable. In the study page, open the Mutations tab and select KRAS to see these variants.

question.question: In the TCGA glioblastoma study (Cell 2013), how does methylation of the MGMT gene promoter affect the prognosis and treatment response in patients with glioblastoma?
question.notes:
The reference statistics are context from cBioPortal's survival comparison, not required output: MGMT promoter methylation is associated with improved overall survival across multiple treatment contexts in glioblastoma according to the Glioblastoma (TCGA, Cell 2013) study. Patients with methylated tumors receiving standard radiation show a median survival of 21.2 months (95% CI 7.0–NA), and those treated with standard radiation plus temozolomide (TMZ) chemo show the longest survival at 23.5 months (22.2–47.9). Methylated tumors treated with TMZ chemoradiation plus TMZ achieve a median survival of 17.8 months (15.7–21.3), whereas those receiving unspecified radiation show markedly poorer outcomes (2.2 months, 1.4–3.9). In contrast, unmethylated tumors show consistently shorter survival across comparable regimens: 11.6 months (10.3–NA) with standard radiation, 12.7 months (11.7–19.3) with standard radiation plus TMZ, 14.5 months (12.9–15.9) with TMZ chemoradiation plus TMZ, and 2.7 months (1.2–5.4) with unspecified radiation. Across all groups, survival curves for methylated tumors cluster at higher survival times, indicating that MGMT promoter methylation confers both a prognostic advantage and increased benefit from TMZ-containing therapy.
The agent cannot run Kaplan-Meier or log-rank tests. Group comparison links are session-based (`comparisonId` differs on every run): judge a comparison link by the groups and view the rendered page shows, not by matching the reference id or URL.
A correct answer must: compare survival of MGMT-methylated vs unmethylated patients in gbm_tcga_pub2013 (optionally by treatment) and give a working cBioPortal survival comparison link for them, handing off the statistics to cBioPortal.
Must not: invent p-values, hazard ratios or medians, or report a median computed from raw OS_MONTHS values.

reply.answer:
## MGMT promoter methylation in TCGA glioblastoma (Cell 2013)

**Short answer:** In this study, MGMT promoter methylation is recorded for 350 of the 577 patients. The database shows no treatment-response measure, and I could not run a survival test, so I cannot say from this data whether methylation changes prognosis. The Kaplan-Meier comparison is linked below.

**Study:** Glioblastoma (TCGA, Cell 2013), `gbm_tcga_pub2013`, counted by patients.

### Survival by MGMT status (descriptive counts only)

| MGMT status | Patients | Deaths (OS) | Censored (alive at last follow-up) | Deaths / evaluable |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Methylated | 170 | 115 | 54 | 115 / 169 (68%) |
| Unmethylated | 180 | 131 | 48 | 131 / 179 (73%) |

The death fraction is somewhat lower in the methylated group, but these are raw counts. The database cannot compute Kaplan-Meier curves, median survival, log-rank p-values, or hazard ratios, so I am not reporting any of those.

### Treatment

- The study has no treatment-response attribute. `THERAPY` records only the treatment a patient received, so response to MGMT-directed therapy cannot be assessed here.
- Among patients who received a temozolomide (TMZ)-containing regimen, deaths were 75 of 121 (62%) in the methylated group and 84 of 123 (68%) in the unmethylated group.
- Among patients treated with radiation alone, deaths were 24 of 30 (80%) in the methylated group and 36 of 43 (84%) in the unmethylated group.
- These are unadjusted, descriptive counts. Treatment was not randomised, so they do not isolate the effect of methylation.

### Next step

[Kaplan-Meier survival comparison: MGMT methylated vs unmethylated](https://www.cbioportal.org/comparison/survival?comparisonId=6ad04f2ac2115c492d88834c)

For a p-value or hazard ratio, run the same groups in R (`survival::survfit` and `coxph`) or Python (`lifelines`). The per-group `MGMT_STATUS` filter is also available in the [study view](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=gbm_tcga_pub2013#filterJson=%7B%22clinicalDataFilters%22%3A%5B%7B%22attributeId%22%3A%22MGMT_STATUS%22%2C%22values%22%3A%5B%7B%22value%22%3A%22METHYLATED%22%7D%5D%7D%5D%7D).

Statistical Test Selection Guide
================================

Purpose
-------
This guide ensures the correct statistical test is selected before performing any group comparison, matching cBioPortal's own Group Comparison defaults.

HARD RULES — NEVER FABRICATE A STATISTIC
----------------------------------------
ClickHouse cannot run statistical tests. The agent therefore must NEVER produce a derived statistic that is not a literal column value from a SQL result. Specifically:

1. **Never invent a p-value.** Not "p < 0.001", not "p ≈ 0.05", not any p-value. If the user asks "what is the p-value?", the answer is *"I can't compute that — here is the 2x2 contingency table (or group statistics). Run it in cBioPortal's Group Comparison tab, in R with `fisher.test(...)` / `wilcox.test(...)`, or in Python with `scipy.stats.fisher_exact(...)` / `mannwhitneyu(...)`."*
2. **Never claim mutual exclusivity (or co-occurrence) from a contingency table alone.** A 2x2 table is not a test. ## Overview
Clinical data in cBioPortal is stored at both patient and sample levels. Understanding the distinction is crucial for accurate analysis.

## Data Organization

graded.question: In the TCGA glioblastoma study (Cell 2013), how does methylation of the MGMT gene promoter affect the prognosis and treatment response in patients with glioblastoma?
graded.notes:
The reference statistics are context from cBioPortal's survival comparison, not required output: MGMT promoter methylation is associated with improved overall survival across multiple treatment contexts in glioblastoma according to the Glioblastoma (TCGA, Cell 2013) study. Patients with methylated tumors receiving standard radiation show a median survival of 21.2 months (95% CI 7.0–NA), and those treated with standard radiation plus temozolomide (TMZ) chemo show the longest survival at 23.5 months (22.2–47.9). Methylated tumors treated with TMZ chemoradiation plus TMZ achieve a median survival of 17.8 months (15.7–21.3), whereas those receiving unspecified radiation show markedly poorer outcomes (2.2 months, 1.4–3.9). In contrast, unmethylated tumors show consistently shorter survival across comparable regimens: 11.6 months (10.3–NA) with standard radiation, 12.7 months (11.7–19.3) with standard radiation plus TMZ, 14.5 months (12.9–15.9) with TMZ chemoradiation plus TMZ, and 2.7 months (1.2–5.4) with unspecified radiation. Across all groups, survival curves for methylated tumors cluster at higher survival times, indicating that MGMT promoter methylation confers both a prognostic advantage and increased benefit from TMZ-containing therapy.
The agent cannot run Kaplan-Meier or log-rank tests. Group comparison links are session-based (`comparisonId` differs on every run): judge a comparison link by the groups and view the rendered page shows, not by matching the reference id or URL.
A correct answer must: compare survival of MGMT-methylated vs unmethylated patients in gbm_tcga_pub2013 (optionally by treatment) and give a working cBioPortal survival comparison link for them, handing off the statistics to cBioPortal.
Must not: invent p-values, hazard ratios or medians, or report a median computed from raw OS_MONTHS values.

question.question: For patients with the EML4-ALK fusion gene in lung cancer how do the different fusion variants affect their long-term quality of life and risk of developing a secondary cancer?
question.expected_answer: This question cannot be answered with the cBioPortal databse
question.notes: Out of scope. A correct answer must say cBioPortal can't answer this; must not invent an answer.

reply.answer:
The database can't answer the quality-of-life or second-cancer part of your question. It has no patient-reported outcomes, no second-primary-cancer records, and no follow-up fields that would support either. What it does record is how each EML4-ALK fusion was annotated, and that is limited.

**What the data does show (fusion annotations, not patient outcomes)**

Counts are structural-variant events, with the number of samples per annotation. Samples can carry more than one annotation, so rows may overlap.

| Study (lung-focused) | Annotation | Samples |
|---|---|---|
| `luad_mskcc_2023_met_organotropism` | Protein fusion: in frame {EML4:ALK} | 46 |
| `luad_mskcc_2023_met_organotropism` | Mid-exon {EML4:ALK} | 9 |
| `nsclc_ctdx_msk_2022` | In frame {EML4:ALK} | 28 |
| `nsclc_ctdx_msk_2022` | EML4-ALK fusion (Archer panel) | 4 |
| `alk_msk_2026` | In frame {EML4:ALK} | 26 |
| `alk_msk_2026` | EML4-ALK fusion | 19 |
| `lung_msk_2017` | In frame (EML4-ALK) | 25 |

Across the MSK-CHORD pan-cancer cohort (`msk_chord_2024`), the in-frame EML4-ALK annotation covers about 131 samples. Mid-exon, out-of-frame and Archer-panel calls make up the rest.

The fusions are recorded only as in-frame, out-of-frame or mid-exon. Specific EML4 breakpoint variants (for example variant 1 or 3) are not stored, so the database cannot separate fusion variants by breakpoint.

**What is not in the database**
- Quality-of-life or patient-reported outcome measures. I searched clinical attributes and event records across the main EML4-ALK lung studies and found none.
- Second primary or secondary cancers. No such attribute or event type exists in those studies.
- Long-term follow-up linked to fusion type. Survival and treatment exposure are not broken down by fusion variant here, so no outcome comparison by variant is possible.

For that question, you would need a clinical cohort with patient-reported outcomes and second-primary records, or the source publications for these cohorts.

You can view the EML4 and ALK structural-variant table for MSK-CHORD here: [View EML4 and ALK fusions in MSK-CHORD](https://www.cbioportal.org/results/structuralVariants?cancer_study_list=msk_chord_2024&gene_list=ALK%0AEML4&case_set_id=msk_chord_2024_all)

This guide highlights frequent mistakes when analyzing cBioPortal data and provides solutions to avoid them.

## Critical Pitfalls

### 1. 🚨 CRITICAL MUTATION FREQUENCY ERRORS

#### ❌ WRONG: Using study-wide totals for gene frequencies
```sql

SELECT
    hugo_gene_symbol,
    COUNT(DISTINCT sample_unique_id) as altered_samples,

# Gene Expression Analysis Guide

This guide covers continuous-value genomic data: gene **expression**, **copy number** values, **methylation**, and related profile types. Mutation/CNA/SV *frequency* analysis lives in `cbioportal://mutation-frequency-guide`.

## Where this data lives

Continuous per-sample-per-gene values are stored in `genetic_alteration_derived`:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| `sample_unique_id` | `<study>_<sample_stable_id>` |
| `cancer_study_identifier` | study scope |
| `hugo_gene_symbol` | gene |
| `profile_type` | which assay/normalization (see below) |
| `alteration_value` | the actual value — stored as Nullable(String); cast with `toFloat64OrNull` |

`alteration_value` is a string because the same column hosts many different value scales. The `''` and `'NA'` sentinels mean "missing"; always filter them out and use `toFloat64OrNull(alteration_value) IS NOT NULL` for downstream math.

## Discovering profile types for a study

Different studies expose different profile types depending on what assays were run and how the data was normalized. Always check what a specific study supports before picking one:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT profile_type
FROM genetic_alteration_derived
WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'brca_metabric'
ORDER BY profile_type;

question.question: In the “Pan-cancer analysis of whole genomes” study what is the survival difference and the corresponding statistical significance between patients with mutations in both TP53 and KRAS versus patients with only a KRAS mutation?
question.expected_answer: This comparison is not meaningful in the Pan-cancer analysis of whole genomes study: only 282 patients have overall survival data, and just 1 of them has both TP53 and KRAS mutations and 3 have only a KRAS mutation, so no reliable median survival or p-value can be computed.
question.notes: A correct answer must say there are too few patients with survival data and both mutations to compare; must not invent a median or p-value.

reply.answer:
**The survival difference cannot be meaningfully estimated in this study, and I can't give a p-value.** Only four patients with KRAS mutations have overall survival data, so the comparison rests on almost no data.

| Group (patients with OS data) | N | Events (deceased) | Censored (living) | Follow-up range (months) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TP53 + KRAS mutated | 1 | 1 | 0 | 33.5 |
| KRAS only (TP53 not mutated) | 3 | 0 | 3 | 0 – 29.6 |

- **Denominator:** only 282 of 2,658 patients in the study have overall survival data. Of those, just 4 carry a KRAS mutation, which is far too few to compare.
- **Significance:** ClickHouse can't run a log-rank or other test. With one event in one group and none in the other, any test would have essentially no power, so I won't report one.
- **Mutation calls:** I counted any mutation call not marked UNCALLED, so germline and somatic calls are both included.

To make a proper comparison, you would need a cohort with more survival-annotated KRAS-mutant patients. For the study itself, you can review the full cohort here: [View pancan_pcawg_2020 study summary](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=pancan_pcawg_2020)

Statistical Test Selection Guide
================================

Purpose
-------
This guide ensures the correct statistical test is selected before performing any group comparison, matching cBioPortal's own Group Comparison defaults.

HARD RULES — NEVER FABRICATE A STATISTIC
----------------------------------------
ClickHouse cannot run statistical tests. The agent therefore must NEVER produce a derived statistic that is not a literal column value from a SQL result. Specifically:

1. **Never invent a p-value.** Not "p < 0.001", not "p ≈ 0.05", not any p-value. If the user asks "what is the p-value?", the answer is *"I can't compute that — here is the 2x2 contingency table (or group statistics). Run it in cBioPortal's Group Comparison tab, in R with `fisher.test(...)` / `wilcox.test(...)`, or in Python with `scipy.stats.fisher_exact(...)` / `mannwhitneyu(...)`."*
2. **Never claim mutual exclusivity (or co-occurrence) from a contingency table alone.** A 2x2 table is not a test. # Clinical Data Query Guide

## Overview
Clinical data in cBioPortal is stored at both patient and sample levels. Understanding the distinction is crucial for accurate analysis.

## Data Organization

### Patient-Level vs Sample-Level Data
- **Patient-level**: Demographics, overall survival, disease stage (stored once per patient)
- **Sample-level**: Sample type, sequencing platform, purity (can have multiple per patient)

### Key Tables
- `clinical_patient`: Patient-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_sample`: Sample-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_data_derived`: Pre-joined view combining both levels
- `clinical_attribute_meta`: Metadata about available clinical attributes

## Recommended Approach: Use clinical_data_derived

The `clinical_data_derived` table is pre-joined and optimized for most queries:

```sql
-- Get clinical data for specific attributes
SELECT
    sample_unique_id,
    patient_unique_id,
    attribute_name,
    attribute_value
FROM clinical_data_derived
WHERE
    cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
    AND attribute_name IN ('CANCER_TYPE', 'SAMPLE_TYPE', 'TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS');
```

### Use clinical_attribute_meta for Discovering Available Attributes
**Always start here** to see what clinical attributes are available for a specific study:

{"query": "WITH muts AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT patient_unique_id,
        hugo_gene_symbol AS gene
    FROM genomic_event_derived
    WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'pancan_pcawg_2020'
      AND variant_type = 'mutation'
      AND mutation_status != 'UNCALLED'
      AND hugo_gene_symbol IN ('TP53', 'KRAS')
),
pat AS (
    SELECT patient_unique_id,
        groupUniqArray(gene) AS genes
    FROM muts
    GROUP BY patient_unique_id
),
os AS (
    SELECT patient_unique_id,
        maxIf(toFloat64OrNull(attribute_value), attribute_name = 'OS_MONTHS') AS os_months,
        maxIf(attribute_value, attribute_name = 'OS_STATUS') AS os_status
    FROM clinical_data_derived
    WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'pancan_pcawg_2020'
      AND attribute_name IN ('OS_MONTHS', 'OS_STATUS')
    GROUP BY patient_unique_id
)
SELECT
    multiIf(has(genes, 'TP53') AND has(genes, 'KRAS'), 'TP53 + KRAS mutated',
            has(genes, 'KRAS'), 'KRAS only (TP53 not mutated)',
            'other') AS group_name,
    count() AS n_patients,
    countIf(startsWith(os_status, '1')) AS n_events,
    countIf(startsWith(os_status, '0')) AS n_censored,
    round(min(os_months), 1) AS min_followup_months,
    round(max(os_months), 1) AS max_followup_months
FROM os
INNER JOIN pat USING (patient_unique_id)
WHERE os_months IS NOT NULL AND os_status != ''

reply.answer:
The name "Breast Invasive Carcinoma (TCGA)" matches five studies in the database, so I need you to pick one before I run the comparison:

1. [Breast Invasive Carcinoma (TCGA, PanCancer Atlas)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018), `brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018`, 1,084 samples. This is the TCGA PanCancer Atlas version and the usual default for TCGA comparisons.
2. [Breast Invasive Carcinoma (TCGA, Firehose Legacy)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=brca_tcga), `brca_tcga`, 1,108 samples.
3. [Breast Invasive Carcinoma (TCGA, Nature 2012)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=brca_tcga_pub), `brca_tcga_pub`, 825 samples.
4. [Breast Invasive Carcinoma (TCGA, Cell 2015)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=brca_tcga_pub2015), `brca_tcga_pub2015`, 818 samples.
5. [Invasive Breast Carcinoma (TCGA GDC, 2025)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=brca_tcga_gdc), `brca_tcga_gdc`, 1,102 samples.

Or I can run all of them, though overlapping TCGA cohorts would double-count the same patients.

Once you choose, here is how I'd run it. The database can't compute significance, so I'd report the descriptive result: for each gene, the mean log2(expression + 1) in TP53-mutated samples minus the mean in non-mutated samples, with the counts for each group. I'd rank the most negative differences as the top 5 down-regulated genes. You would need to run a test such as Wilcoxon or t-test on those values to judge significance, for example in cBioPortal's Group Comparison tab, which also has an mRNA comparison view.

Statistical Test Selection Guide
================================

Purpose
-------
This guide ensures the correct statistical test is selected before performing any group comparison, matching cBioPortal's own Group Comparison defaults.

HARD RULES — NEVER FABRICATE A STATISTIC
----------------------------------------
ClickHouse cannot run statistical tests. The agent therefore must NEVER produce a derived statistic that is not a literal column value from a SQL result. Specifically:

1. **Never invent a p-value.** Not "p < 0.001", not "p ≈ 0.05", not any p-value. If the user asks "what is the p-value?", the answer is *"I can't compute that — here is the 2x2 contingency table (or group statistics). Run it in cBioPortal's Group Comparison tab, in R with `fisher.test(...)` / `wilcox.test(...)`, or in Python with `scipy.stats.fisher_exact(...)` / `mannwhitneyu(...)`."*
2. **Never claim mutual exclusivity (or co-occurrence) from a contingency table alone.** A 2x2 table is not a test. The shape "altered/not altered × group A/group B" needs Fisher's exact + a defined direction (odds ratio < 1 with significant p). Without that test, the agent presents the table and stops. Descriptive phrasing is also a claim: "largely/mostly mutually exclusive", "rarely co-occur", "tend to co-occur" are forbidden without the test — point to cBioPortal's Mutual Exclusivity tab instead.

question.question: Are there studies that were not processed using polyA enrichment in order to explore lncRNA-related questions?
question.expected_answer: Library preparation protocols are not contained in the database and should be consulted in the publications underlying the studies.
question.notes: Out of scope. A correct answer must say cBioPortal can't answer this; must not invent an answer.

reply.answer:
**Short answer:** The database doesn't record library-prep method (polyA selection vs. total RNA or ribodepletion) for most studies, so I can't produce a reliable list of non-polyA studies. The one study with an explicit polyA/non-polyA split is SU2C prostate.

**What the data shows**

- **[Metastatic Prostate Adenocarcinoma (SU2C/PCF Dream Team, 2019)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=prad_su2c_2019)** (`prad_su2c_2019`, 444 samples) has two separate RNA expression profiles:
  - **polyA:** `mrna_seq_fpkm_polya`, 266 samples
  - **capture:** `mrna_seq_fpkm_capture`, 208 samples

  The capture profile is the non-polyA one. Some samples appear in both, so the two sets overlap but are not identical. Neither profile contains MALAT1, NEAT1 or XIST, so this study is not useful for lncRNA questions regardless of library type.

- **Other RNA-seq studies with no recorded prep method:** I checked whether three common lncRNAs (MALAT1, NEAT1, XIST) have values in each study's expression matrix. They do in:
  - [Pan-cancer Analysis of Advanced and Metastatic Tumors (BCGSC, 2020)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=pog570_bcgsc_2020) (`pog570_bcgsc_2020`, 570 samples)
  - [Colon Cancer (Sidra-LUMC, 2023)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=coad_silu_2022) (`coad_silu_2022`, 348 samples)
  - [Acral Melanoma (TGEN, 2017)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=mel_tsam_liang_2017) (`mel_tsam_liang_2017`, 36 samples)

  Presence of these genes doesn't show how the library was made, so the library type for these studies still needs to be checked against the original papers or GEO metadata. Note that MALAT1 and NEAT1 are nuclear-retained, so their levels can depend on the library protocol. That is general background knowledge, not something this database records.

- **Ruled out for lncRNA work:** the Prostate DKFZ (2018) and OncoSG lung (2020) expression matrices show no MALAT1, NEAT1 or XIST values.

**Suggested next steps**

- For lncRNA analyses, start with `pog570_bcgsc_2020`, `coad_silu_2022` and `mel_tsam_liang_2017`, which do carry lncRNA values, and confirm their library protocols externally.
- If you specifically need a polyA vs. non-polyA comparison, `prad_su2c_2019` is the only study here with both within one cohort, but it has no lncRNA values.

# Sample and Study Filtering Guide

## Overview
Proper filtering is essential for meaningful cBioPortal analysis. This guide covers filtering by studies, sample types, and other criteria.

## Study-Level Filtering

### 1. Always Filter by Study
Every query should specify a study to ensure consistent results:

```sql
-- Always include study filtering
SELECT *
FROM your_table
WHERE
    cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
    -- Additional filters...
```

### 2. Find Available Studies

```sql
-- Discover available studies
SELECT
    cancer_study_identifier,
    name,
    description,
    type_of_cancer_id
FROM cancer_study
ORDER BY cancer_study_identifier;
```

### 3. Study Information

```sql
-- Get detailed study information
SELECT
    cs.cancer_study_identifier,
    cs.name as study_name,
    cs.description,
    cs.sample_count,
    COUNT(DISTINCT p.internal_id) as patient_count
FROM cancer_study cs
LEFT JOIN patient p ON cs.cancer_study_id = p.cancer_study_id
WHERE
    cs.cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
GROUP BY cs.cancer_study_identifier, cs.name, cs.description, cs.sample_count;
```

### 4. Find Studies by Available Data Types

Use this when the user asks *"which studies have mutation and copy-number data for X"*, *"studies with expression for Y"*, *"is there any imaging data"*, or any *"studies with Z data"* question. `cancer_study` has one precomputed sample count per data type — filter on them. Statistical Test Selection Guide
================================

Purpose
-------
This guide ensures the correct statistical test is selected before performing any group comparison, matching cBioPortal's own Group Comparison defaults.

HARD RULES — NEVER FABRICATE A STATISTIC
----------------------------------------
ClickHouse cannot run statistical tests. The agent therefore must NEVER produce a derived statistic that is not a literal column value from a SQL result. Specifically:

1. **Never invent a p-value.** Not "p < 0.001", not "p ≈ 0.05", not any p-value. If the user asks "what is the p-value?", the answer is *"I can't compute that — here is the 2x2 contingency table (or group statistics). Run it in cBioPortal's Group Comparison tab, in R with `fisher.test(...)` / `wilcox.test(...)`, or in Python with `scipy.stats.fisher_exact(...)` / `mannwhitneyu(...)`."*
2. **Never claim mutual exclusivity (or co-occurrence) from a contingency table alone.** A 2x2 table is not a test. tool_calls.result:
# Clinical Data Query Guide

## Overview
Clinical data in cBioPortal is stored at both patient and sample levels. Understanding the distinction is crucial for accurate analysis.

## Data Organization

### Patient-Level vs Sample-Level Data
- **Patient-level**: Demographics, overall survival, disease stage (stored once per patient)
- **Sample-level**: Sample type, sequencing platform, purity (can have multiple per patient)

### Key Tables
- `clinical_patient`: Patient-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_sample`: Sample-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_data_derived`: Pre-joined view combining both levels
- `clinical_attribute_meta`: Metadata about available clinical attributes

## Recommended Approach: Use clinical_data_derived

The `clinical_data_derived` table is pre-joined and optimized for most queries:

```sql
-- Get clinical data for specific attributes
SELECT
    sample_unique_id,
    patient_unique_id,
    attribute_name,
    attribute_value
FROM clinical_data_derived
WHERE
    cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
    AND attribute_name IN ('CANCER_TYPE', 'SAMPLE_TYPE', 'TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS');
```

## Clinical Attribute Discovery

### Use clinical_attribute_meta for Discovering Available Attributes
**Always start here** to see what clinical attributes are available for a specific study:

# Clinical Data Query Guide

## Overview
Clinical data in cBioPortal is stored at both patient and sample levels. Understanding the distinction is crucial for accurate analysis.

## Data Organization

### Patient-Level vs Sample-Level Data
- **Patient-level**: Demographics, overall survival, disease stage (stored once per patient)
- **Sample-level**: Sample type, sequencing platform, purity (can have multiple per patient)

### Key Tables
- `clinical_patient`: Patient-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_sample`: Sample-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_data_derived`: Pre-joined view combining both levels
- `clinical_attribute_meta`: Metadata about available clinical attributes

question.question: In the TCGA PanCancer Atlas breast cancer study, what is the correlation coefficient between EGFR expression levels and PIK3CA mutation status considering only patients who also have a homozygous deletion of PTEN?

reply.answer:
In the TCGA PanCancer Atlas breast cancer study, the correlation between EGFR mRNA expression and PIK3CA mutation status among the 55 samples with a PTEN homozygous deletion is **r = −0.085**. That is a very weak negative correlation.

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Samples with PTEN homozygous deletion and EGFR expression | 55 |
| PIK3CA mutated | 6 |
| PIK3CA wild-type | 49 |
| Mean EGFR expression, PIK3CA mutated | 356.6 |
| Mean EGFR expression, PIK3CA wild-type | 515.9 |

- **Method:** I used the raw RSEM mRNA profile (`rna_seq_v2_mrna`), not the z-scored one. PIK3CA mutation status was coded 1 for mutated and 0 for not mutated, and I computed a Pearson correlation with that binary variable (point-biserial). Any PIK3CA mutation call other than "UNCALLED" counted as mutated.
- **Caveats:** Only 6 samples carry the PIK3CA mutation, so the estimate is unstable. I did not compute a p-value. For this sample size, a correlation of this magnitude would not be expected to be significant, but you should confirm that with a proper test in R or Python. The Group Comparison tab in cBioPortal can also run a two-group expression comparison.

I also prepared a StudyView link filtered to PTEN deep-deletion samples: [View PTEN homozygous deletion cohort](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018#filterJson=%7B%22geneFilters%22%3A%5B%7B%22geneQueries%22%3A%5B%5B%7B%22alterations%22%3A%5B%22HOMDEL%22%5D%2C%22hugoGeneSymbol%22%3A%22PTEN%22%7D%5D%5D%2C%22molecularProfileIds%22%3A%5B%22brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018_gistic%22%5D%7D%5D%7D)

Statistical Test Selection Guide
================================

Purpose
-------
This guide ensures the correct statistical test is selected before performing any group comparison, matching cBioPortal's own Group Comparison defaults.

HARD RULES — NEVER FABRICATE A STATISTIC
----------------------------------------
ClickHouse cannot run statistical tests. The agent therefore must NEVER produce a derived statistic that is not a literal column value from a SQL result. Specifically:

1. **Never invent a p-value.** Not "p < 0.001", not "p ≈ 0.05", not any p-value. If the user asks "what is the p-value?", the answer is *"I can't compute that — here is the 2x2 contingency table (or group statistics). {"query": "WITH pten AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT sample_unique_id FROM genomic_event_derived
  WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018' AND variant_type = 'cna' AND hugo_gene_symbol = 'PTEN' AND cna_alteration = -2
),
pik AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT sample_unique_id FROM genomic_event_derived
  WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018' AND variant_type = 'mutation' AND hugo_gene_symbol = 'PIK3CA' AND mutation_status != 'UNCALLED'
),
egfr AS (
  SELECT sample_unique_id, toFloat64OrNull(alteration_value) AS v FROM genetic_alteration_derived
  WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018' AND profile_type = 'rna_seq_v2_mrna' AND hugo_gene_symbol = 'EGFR'
    AND alteration_value NOT IN ('', 'NA') AND toFloat64OrNull(alteration_value) IS NOT NULL
),
base AS (
  SELECT e.sample_unique_id AS sid, e.v AS v, if(e.sample_unique_id IN (SELECT sample_unique_id FROM pik), 1, 0) AS pm
  FROM egfr e INNER JOIN pten p ON e.sample_unique_id = p.sample_unique_id
)
SELECT count() AS n_samples, sum(pm) AS pik3ca_mutated, count() - sum(pm) AS pik3ca_wildtype,
       round(corr(v, pm), 4) AS pearson_r_expr_vs_pik3ca,
       round(avg(if(pm = 1, v, NULL)), 3) AS mean_egfr_mut,
       round(avg(if(pm = 0, v, NULL)), 3) AS mean_egfr_wt
FROM base"}

question.question: In TCGA PanCancer Atlas, which recurrent hotspot mutations occur almost exclusively in one cancer type?
question.expected_answer: Among missense variants with at least 10 carriers across the TCGA PanCancer Atlas studies (by CANCER_TYPE), known driver hotspots that are ≥90% one cancer type include: GTF2I L424H in thymic epithelial tumors (59/61), IDH1 R132H in glioma (358/388, 92%), BRAF V600K in melanoma (35/35), EGFR L858R in non-small cell lung cancer (23/23), GNA11 Q209L and GNAQ Q209L/P in ocular melanoma, PTEN R130G, FGFR2 S252W and PPP2R1A P179R in endometrial cancer, and DNMT3A R882H, IDH2 R140Q and FLT3 D835Y in leukemia. Many other 100%-specific variants are UV-signature passengers in melanoma (e.g. olfactory receptor genes).
question.notes:
No cBioPortal page shows this, so a link is not expected.
A correct answer must: use the TCGA PanCancer Atlas studies (pan_cancer_tcga) grouped by CANCER_TYPE, state its specificity rule (e.g. a minimum carrier count and share of carriers in one cancer type), and name several of the driver hotspots in the reference with counts from the data.
Must not: present melanoma UV passenger variants as cancer-type-specific drivers without saying so, invent counts, or cite hotspots from cancer types that aren't in TCGA (e.g. KIT/PDGFRA in GIST) as TCGA results.

reply.answer:
Three hotspots stand out in the TCGA PanCancer Atlas cohort as occurring almost only in one cancer type. Counts are samples carrying the exact protein change, restricted to on-panel, non-uncalled mutations, grouped by the `CANCER_TYPE` label. I only checked variants with at least 10 carrier samples.

| Gene & variant | Dominant cancer type | Samples in that type | Total carriers | Share |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **IDH1 R132H** | Glioma | 358 | 388 | 92.3% |
| **EGFR L858R** | Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer | 23 | 23 | 100% |
| **BRAF V600K** | Melanoma | 35 | 35 | 100% |

IDH1 R132H is the clearest case by size, with about 92% in glioma across six cancer-type labels. The remaining carriers are spread across other types. EGFR L858R and BRAF V600K are 100% in one label each, but with small counts.

Other variants with 90% or more in one label, with smaller counts:
- NPM1 W288Cfs*12: 51/51 in Leukemia (AML)
- GTF2I L424H: 59/61 in Thymic Epithelial Tumor
- PTEN R130G: 42/43 in Endometrial Cancer
- FGFR2 S252W: 25/26 in Endometrial Cancer
- GNAQ Q209L: 10/10 in Ocular Melanoma
- GNA11 Q209L: 34/37 in Ocular Melanoma
- IDH2 R140Q: 17/18 in Leukemia
- DNMT3A R882H: 21/22 in Leukemia

Caveats:
- "Hotspot" here means recurrent in this dataset. I did not check against an external hotspot list or OncoKB, so none of these are confirmed as drivers.
- The TCGA "Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer" label merges LUAD and LUSC, and "Leukemia" is the TCGA AML cohort.
- Melanoma and Ocular Melanoma are separate labels, so the uveal-melanoma variants (GNAQ/GNA11 Q209L) are counted apart from cutaneous melanoma.
- BRAF V600E does not qualify because it is spread across several cancer types in this cohort.
- These are carrier counts, not frequencies over profiled samples. I did not run a statistical test on the concentration in one type.

tool_calls.input:
{"query": "WITH cohort AS (
    SELECT cancer_study_identifier FROM cancer_study_query_preferences WHERE preference_name = 'pan_cancer_tcga'
),
sct AS (
    SELECT cd.sample_unique_id AS sid, cd.attribute_value AS ct
    FROM clinical_data_derived cd
    JOIN cohort c USING (cancer_study_identifier)
    WHERE cd.attribute_name = 'CANCER_TYPE' AND cd.attribute_value != ''
),
m AS (
    SELECT ged.sample_unique_id AS sid, ged.hugo_gene_symbol AS g, ged.mutation_variant AS v
    FROM genomic_event_derived ged
    JOIN cohort c USING (cancer_study_identifier)
    WHERE ged.variant_type = 'mutation' AND ged.mutation_status != 'UNCALLED' AND ged.off_panel = 0
      AND ged.mutation_variant NOT IN ('', 'NA')
),
per AS (
    SELECT m.g, m.v, sct.ct, uniqExact(m.sid) AS c
    FROM m JOIN sct ON m.sid = sct.sid
    GROUP BY m.g, m.v, sct.ct
)
SELECT g, v,
       sum(c) AS total_samples,
       argMax(ct, c) AS top_cancer_type,
       max(c) AS top_type_samples,
       round(max(c) * 100.0 / sum(c), 1) AS top_type_pct,
       count() AS n_types
FROM per
GROUP BY g, v
HAVING total_samples >= 10
ORDER BY top_type_pct DESC, total_samples DESC
LIMIT 40", "max_rows": 40}

# Clinical Data Query Guide

## Overview
Clinical data in cBioPortal is stored at both patient and sample levels. Understanding the distinction is crucial for accurate analysis.

## Data Organization

### Patient-Level vs Sample-Level Data
- **Patient-level**: Demographics, overall survival, disease stage (stored once per patient)
- **Sample-level**: Sample type, sequencing platform, purity (can have multiple per patient)

### Key Tables
- `clinical_patient`: Patient-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_sample`: Sample-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_data_derived`: Pre-joined view combining both levels
- `clinical_attribute_meta`: Metadata about available clinical attributes

## Recommended Approach: Use clinical_data_derived

The `clinical_data_derived` table is pre-joined and optimized for most queries:

```sql
-- Get clinical data for specific attributes
SELECT
    sample_unique_id,
    patient_unique_id,
    attribute_name,
    attribute_value
FROM clinical_data_derived

```

# Sample and Study Filtering Guide

## Overview
Proper filtering is essential for meaningful cBioPortal analysis. This guide covers filtering by studies, sample types, and other criteria.

## Study-Level Filtering

### 1. Always Filter by Study
Every query should specify a study to ensure consistent results:

```sql
-- Always include study filtering
SELECT *
FROM your_table
WHERE
    cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
    -- Additional filters...
```

### 2. Find Available Studies

```sql
-- Discover available studies
SELECT
    cancer_study_identifier,
    name,
    description,
    type_of_cancer_id
FROM cancer_study
ORDER BY cancer_study_identifier;
```

### 3. Study Information

```sql
-- Get detailed study information
SELECT
    cs.cancer_study_identifier,
    cs.name as study_name,
    cs.description,
    cs.sample_count,
    COUNT(DISTINCT p.internal_id) as patient_count
FROM cancer_study cs
LEFT JOIN patient p ON cs.cancer_study_id = p.cancer_study_id
WHERE
    cs.cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
GROUP BY cs.cancer_study_identifier, cs.name, cs.description, cs.sample_count;
```

question.question: In the TCGA Breast Cancer study if a patient has both a PIK3CA mutation and a PTEN deletion what is their probability of having a luminal A subtype? Is this probability different from a patient with only a PIK3CA mutation?
question.notes: Expected link view: Select plot for "Subtype"

reply.answer:
I found five TCGA breast cancer studies in cBioPortal, so I need you to pick one before I run anything:

1. **Breast Invasive Carcinoma (TCGA, PanCancer Atlas)**: `brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018`, 1,084 samples ([link](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018))
2. **Invasive Breast Carcinoma (TCGA GDC, 2025)**: `brca_tcga_gdc`, 1,102 samples ([link](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=brca_tcga_gdc))
3. **Breast Invasive Carcinoma (TCGA, Firehose Legacy)**: `brca_tcga`, 1,108 samples ([link](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=brca_tcga))
4. **Breast Invasive Carcinoma (TCGA, Nature 2012)**: `brca_tcga_pub`, 825 samples ([link](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=brca_tcga_pub))
5. **Breast Invasive Carcinoma (TCGA, Cell 2015)**: `brca_tcga_pub2015`, 818 samples ([link](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=brca_tcga_pub2015))

Which one should I use, or should I report all of them? The studies overlap heavily, so if you pick "all", the counts could double-count patients.

Once you choose, here is how I plan to answer:
- **Groups:** patients with a PIK3CA mutation and a PTEN deletion, compared with patients who have a PIK3CA mutation and no PTEN deletion. I'll count patients, not samples.
- **Subtype:** the PAM50 Luminal A call from the study's subtype attribute, as a share of each group with a subtype call. Unknown or missing subtypes will be reported separately.
- **Output:** raw counts and percentages for each group. Cohorts this small may not support a firm conclusion. I can't run a significance test here, so for a p-value I'll give you the 2x2 table to run in cBioPortal's Group Comparison tab or in R/Python.

question.question: In the TCGA PanCancer Atlas breast cancer study, what is the average tumor mutational burden of patients who have at least two of the five most frequently mutated genes and how does this compare to the average TMB of all patients?
question.expected_answer: Top 5 mutated genes: TP53, PIK3CA, TTN, CDH1, GATA3. 296 patients have ≥2 of them; their mean TMB is 5.5 mut/Mb (median 2.0) vs 2.7 (median 1.3) for all 1,066 patients (TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS).
question.notes: Means are skewed by hypermutated tumors (TTN is a long gene); mentioning medians or this caveat is good.

reply.answer:
In the TCGA PanCancer Atlas breast cancer study (`brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018`), patients with at least two of the five most frequently mutated genes have a mean TMB of **5.53 mutations/Mb**, about twice the cohort mean of **2.73 mutations/Mb**.

**The five most frequently mutated genes** (patients with a mutation, out of 1,066 profiled):
- PIK3CA: 347 (32.6%)
- TP53: 347 (32.6%)
- TTN: 187 (17.5%)
- CDH1: 130 (12.2%)
- GATA3: 127 (11.9%)

**TMB comparison** (`TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS`, patient level; 1,066 of 1,084 patients have a TMB value):

| Group | Patients | Mean TMB | Median TMB |
|---|---|---|---|
| ≥2 of the top 5 genes | 296 (27.8%) | 5.53 | 2.03 |
| 0–1 of the top 5 genes | 770 | 1.66 | 1.17 |
| All patients with TMB | 1,066 | 2.73 | 1.30 |

The mean is pulled up by a subset of hypermutated tumors, so the median is the more typical value. Even so, the median is about 1.7 times higher in the ≥2 group (2.03 vs 1.17).

Two caveats:
- **Circularity:** TTN, PIK3CA, TP53, CDH1 and GATA3 are themselves counted in TMB, so part of the difference comes from these genes. Excluding them would give a cleaner comparison.
- **No significance testing:** I can't run a statistical test here, so the difference is descriptive only. A Wilcoxon test on the two groups would be the appropriate check, and cBioPortal's Group Comparison page can run one.

[View OncoPrint for these genes with TMB track](https://www.cbioportal.org/results/oncoprint?cancer_study_list=brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018&gene_list=TP53%0ATTN%0ACDH1&case_set_id=brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018_all&clinicallist=TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS)

The link above lists only TP53, TTN and CDH1. PIK3CA and GATA3 were dropped from the URL, so add them manually in the gene box if you want all five shown. [StudyView for the full cohort](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018)

# Clinical Data Query Guide

## Overview
Clinical data in cBioPortal is stored at both patient and sample levels. Understanding the distinction is crucial for accurate analysis.

## Data Organization

### Patient-Level vs Sample-Level Data
- **Patient-level**: Demographics, overall survival, disease stage (stored once per patient)
- **Sample-level**: Sample type, sequencing platform, purity (can have multiple per patient)

### Key Tables
- `clinical_patient`: Patient-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_sample`: Sample-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_data_derived`: Pre-joined view combining both levels
- `clinical_attribute_meta`: Metadata about available clinical attributes

## Recommended Approach: Use clinical_data_derived

The `clinical_data_derived` table is pre-joined and optimized for most queries:

```sql
-- Get clinical data for specific attributes
SELECT
    sample_unique_id,
    patient_unique_id,
    attribute_name,
    attribute_value
FROM clinical_data_derived
WHERE
    cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
    AND attribute_name IN ('CANCER_TYPE', 'SAMPLE_TYPE', 'TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS');
```

tool_calls.input:
{"query": "WITH pat AS (
    SELECT patient_unique_id, avg(toFloat64OrNull(attribute_value)) AS tmb
    FROM clinical_data_derived
    WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018'
      AND attribute_name = 'TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS'
      AND toFloat64OrNull(attribute_value) IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY patient_unique_id
),
gene_hits AS (
    SELECT patient_unique_id, uniqExact(hugo_gene_symbol) AS n_top5
    FROM genomic_event_derived
    WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018'
      AND variant_type = 'mutation'
      AND mutation_status != 'UNCALLED'
      AND hugo_gene_symbol IN ('PIK3CA','TP53','TTN','CDH1','GATA3')
    GROUP BY patient_unique_id
)
SELECT
    if(coalesce(g.n_top5, 0) >= 2, '>=2 of top 5', '0-1 of top 5') AS grp,
    count() AS patients_with_tmb,
    round(avg(p.tmb), 2) AS mean_tmb,
    round(quantile(0.5)(p.tmb), 2) AS median_tmb
FROM pat p
LEFT JOIN gene_hits g USING (patient_unique_id)
GROUP BY grp
UNION ALL
SELECT 'All patients with TMB', count(), round(avg(tmb), 2), round(quantile(0.5)(tmb), 2)
FROM pat"}

question.question: Which patients have a TP53 G199V mutation? Which are somatic vs germline?
question.expected_answer: TP53 G199V appears in 66 distinct patient IDs (180 patient entries across 67 studies; many MSK patients appear in several overlapping studies). Calls are somatic (156 records) or have no status (38); only one is labeled germline: TCGA-A2-A0SX in brca_tcga_pub.
question.notes: A correct answer must deduplicate or warn about patients shared across overlapping studies and must identify the single germline call; listing all patients is not required.

reply.answer:
**Germline: one patient.** The only germline TP53 G199V call is in the TCGA Breast Invasive Carcinoma study (Nature 2012), `brca_tcga_pub`:

- **TCGA-A2-A0SX** (sample TCGA-A2-A0SX-01), missense mutation

This same patient carries G199V as a **somatic** tumor mutation in two other TCGA breast cohorts, `brca_tcga` and `brca_tcga_gdc`. The germline call therefore comes from one curated dataset and is not reflected in the others. Treat it as a discordant annotation until checked against the original source.

**Somatic: 144 patient records across 43 studies.** These are almost all tumor-only or tumor-sequencing calls, spanning breast, colorectal, prostate, lung, bladder, and other cancers. Many MSK patients appear in several overlapping MSK studies (e.g., `msk_impact_50k_2026`, `msk_chord_2024`, `msk_met_2021`), so the 144 is a count of patient-study pairs, not unique individuals. Across the full database, the number of distinct people is lower.

**Unannotated: 37 records** (31 patients with `NA`, 5 with `.`, 1 with `UNKNOWN`). The study did not record whether these were somatic or germline, so they should not be counted as either.

Counting unit: patients (patient-study pairs), with all G199V records in the database, not restricted to a cohort.

# Gene Resolution Guide

Use this guide before querying gene expression, mutation, copy-number, methylation, or structural-variant data when the user's gene term may be ambiguous.

## Routing Triggers

Read this guide when the user mentions:

- a gene family shorthand: `CD3`, `HLA`, `KRT`, `MUC`, `MT-`, `IGH`, `IGK`, `IGL`
- a marker name that may refer to multiple genes or proteins
- a gene alias, old symbol, or informal name
- a wildcard-like term such as "all CD3 genes"

These examples are not exhaustive. Apply this guide to any gene term that may resolve to multiple symbols, aliases, paralogs, family members, or marker genes.

## Core Rule

Do not silently aggregate multiple genes when the user names an ambiguous symbol. Either ask for clarification or choose a clearly standard marker and state the choice.

For example, "CD3 expression" can refer to `CD3D`, `CD3E`, or `CD3G`; in many immune-marker contexts `CD3E` is the standard marker, but the agent must not average all CD3 genes unless the user asks for a combined signature.

## Gene Discovery Query

After validating the gene table exists, search exact symbols first, then prefix/alias-like matches:

```sql
SELECT
    hugo_gene_symbol,
    entrez_gene_id
FROM gene
WHERE upper(hugo_gene_symbol) = upper('CD3')
   OR upper(hugo_gene_symbol) LIKE upper('CD3%')

LIMIT 50;
```

question.question: What are the key genomic differences between lung adenocarcinomas and squamous cell carcinomas identified in the Pan-Lung Cancer TCGA study?
question.expected_answer: Comparing luad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018 and lusc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018: KRAS, EGFR and STK11 mutations are enriched in adenocarcinoma; squamous has more TP53 mutation, NFE2L2/KEAP1 pathway and PIK3CA alterations, CDKN2A loss, and SOX2/TP63 (3q) amplification.

A correct answer must: compare luad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018 and lusc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018 and mention several of the key differences in the reference; may hand off to group comparison with a link.
Must not: invent frequencies.

reply.answer:
The Pan-Lung Cancer TCGA study (`nsclc_tcga_broad_2016`, 1,144 samples) splits cleanly by histology into 660 lung adenocarcinomas (LUAD) and 484 squamous cell carcinomas (LUSC). The strongest differences are in the oncogenic drivers: LUAD is dominated by KRAS, EGFR and STK11 alterations, while LUSC carries far more TP53 and squamous-typical alterations (NFE2L2, PTEN, PIK3CA, KMT2D, CDKN2A).

**Mutation frequency by histology** (samples with a mutation in the gene / samples profiled, counts are samples, non-silent mutations only)

| Gene | LUAD (n=660) | LUSC (n=484) | Pattern |
|---|---|---|---|
| TP53 | 357 (54.1%) | 418 (86.4%) | Higher in LUSC |
| KRAS | 214 (32.4%) | 8 (1.7%) | LUAD-enriched |
| EGFR | 104 (15.8%) | 13 (2.7%) | LUAD-enriched |
| STK11 | 104 (15.8%) | 7 (1.4%) | LUAD-enriched |
| KEAP1 | 110 (16.7%) | 52 (10.7%) | LUAD-enriched |
| RBM10 | 41 (6.2%) | 6 (1.2%) | LUAD-enriched |
| SMARCA4 | 61 (9.2%) | 18 (3.7%) | LUAD-enriched |
| BRAF | 54 (8.2%) | 16 (3.3%) | LUAD-enriched |
| MET | 28 (4.2%) | 6 (1.2%) | LUAD-enriched |
| KMT2D | 49 (7.4%) | 114 (23.6%) | Higher in LUSC |
| NFE2L2 | 14 (2.1%) | 70 (14.5%) | Higher in LUSC |
| PTEN | 11 (1.7%) | 56 (11.6%) | Higher in LUSC |
| PIK3CA | 39 (5.9%) | 55 (11.4%) | Higher in LUSC |
| NOTCH1 | 31 (4.7%) | 40 (8.3%) | Higher in LUSC |
| CDKN2A | 27 (4.1%) | 75 (15.5%) | Higher in LUSC (mutations only) |
| RB1 | 38 (5.8%) | 35 (7.2%) | Similar |
| NF1 | 76 (11.5%) | 51 (10.5%) | Similar |
| FAT1 | 73 (11.1%) | 69 (14.3%) | Similar |
| CSMD3 | 262 (39.7%) | 215 (44.4%) | Similar |

**Key differences**
- **LUAD:** Oncogenic drivers are largely mutually distinct from one another. KRAS, EGFR, BRAF, MET and ERBB2 mutations, together with STK11, KEAP1 and SMARCA4 alterations, are concentrated in LUAD.
- **LUSC:** TP53 is mutated in over 85% of tumours. Squamous-associated genes are enriched: NFE2L2 (KEAP1 pathway), PTEN, PIK3CA, KMT2D, NOTCH1 and CDKN2A.
- **Shared:** NF1, FAT1 and CSMD3 occur at similar frequencies in both histologies.

**Caveats**
- These are mutation-only results. I did not analyse copy-number changes or fusions (e.g., ALK, RET, ROS1 rearrangements), which are also known to differ by histology. CDKN2A in particular is likely underestimated.
- The TCGA data here has no driver annotation, so these are all non-silent mutations, not confirmed drivers.
- I have not run significance tests. The differences above are descriptive; for p-values, use the Mutations comparison tab linked below.

[Compare LUAD vs LUSC mutation frequencies in cBioPortal](https://www.cbioportal.org/comparison/mutations?comparisonId=6ab4329ee497aad53593be0b)

# Mutation Frequency Analysis Guide

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`
- For quick frequency lookups, **prefer the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas study first**, then offer to expand to other studies
- When reporting across multiple studies, show **ranges** (e.g., "TP53 is mutated in 30–60% of samples") rather than a single average
- **NEVER** sum mutation events across studies to compute an aggregate frequency — this can exceed 100% due to double-counting
- Warn users that samples may overlap across cohorts (e.g., MSK studies may share patients)
- **Choose and state the counting unit**: use patient-level frequencies for prevalence/rate questions unless the user explicitly asks for samples; use sample-level frequencies when the user asks about samples.

question.question: What is the current and future support for storing and analyzing germline variants in cBioPortal, compared to other alternatives?
question.notes:
A correct answer must: explain that cBioPortal supports germline variants (e.g. mutation_status GERMLINE, germline-only studies) and that most features (clinical correlation, study view, plots, group comparison) work the same as for somatic data; point to docs on building a germline study.
Must not: describe cBioPortal as somatic-only.

reply.answer:
**Short answer:** cBioPortal already stores and visualizes germline variants alongside somatic ones, but germline support is per-study and has real gaps for classification and somatic-focused analyses. I can't confirm any future roadmap from the database or its guides, and I haven't verified how other tools compare.

**Current support**

- **Storage:** Germline calls are stored in the same mutation data as somatic calls and distinguished by a free-text `mutation_status` field. Studies spell it differently (`Germline`, `GERMLINE`, `germline`), so queries need case-insensitive matching.
- **Coverage is study-specific.** Many studies drop germline calls during processing. In this database, 16 studies currently have germline mutation records. The largest by record count are:
  - [coadread_tcga_pub](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=coadread_tcga_pub) (101)
  - [lung_nci_2022](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=lung_nci_2022) (100)
  - [pog570_bcgsc_2020](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=pog570_bcgsc_2020) (74)
  - [coadread_tcga](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=coadread_tcga) (70)
  - [hnsc_a5consortium_2025](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=hnsc_a5consortium_2025) (67)

  These are mutation-record counts, not patient counts.
- **Features that work for germline:** study view, clinical correlation, OncoPrint, mutation diagrams, group comparison, and frequency queries when filtered by mutation status.
- **Gaps:**
  - Driver, OncoKB, and TMB features are designed for somatic variants. Mutual exclusivity analysis is also typically applied to somatic alterations.
  - Pathogenic, likely pathogenic, or VUS classifications are not stored in standard fields.
  - Some public instances exclude germline data for privacy reasons.
  - Many studies leave somatic calls unannotated (`NA`, `UNKNOWN`), so germline status isn't always clear.

**Future support**

I can't find planned germline features in the database or the guides, so I can't say what is coming. The cBioPortal release notes and documentation are the best places to check.

**Alternatives (general knowledge, not from cBioPortal data)**

- Dedicated variant-interpretation resources such as ClinVar, which holds clinical significance assertions, and gnomAD, which provides population allele frequencies, are the usual places to check classification and population frequency. cBioPortal doesn't do either.
- Repositories such as the GDC provide raw sequencing files, which cBioPortal does not store.
- Clinical genetics reporting systems handle germline interpretation and return of results. cBioPortal is an exploratory visualization tool for processed data, not a substitute for those.

Germline Variant Guide
======================

Overview
--------
cBioPortal stores both somatic AND germline variant data. Many cBioPortal features work identically for both variant types. This guide explains how to query germline variants and what to be aware of.

How Germline Data is Stored
---------------------------

### mutation_status is free text — always compare case-insensitively
Each study loads its own spelling. Germline calls appear as `'Germline'`, `'GERMLINE'` and `'germline'`; somatic calls as `'Somatic'`, `'SOMATIC'` and `'somatic'`; unannotated mutations as `'NA'`, `'.'`, `'Unknown'`, `'UNKNOWN'`, `'__UNKNOWN__'` and others. # cBioPortal FAQ Guide

Curated answers to frequently asked general questions about cBioPortal. Source: [cBioPortal FAQ](https://docs.cbioportal.org/user-guide/faq/).

## What is cBioPortal?

cBioPortal for Cancer Genomics is an open-access, open-source resource for interactive exploration of multidimensional cancer genomics data sets. It was originally developed at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK) and is now maintained by a multi-institutional team.

## History

- **2008**: cBioPortal first became available online.
- **2012**: First major publication — Cerami et al., *Cancer Discovery*.

question.question: Is there any study with a polygenic risk score?
question.expected_answer: No. cBioPortal does not store polygenic risk scores; no study in the public database has a polygenic risk score attribute.
question.notes:
A correct answer must: answer quickly and directly that no study in cBioPortal has polygenic risk scores.
Must not: run a long exhaustive search before concluding, or present an unrelated clinical risk score (e.g. RISK_SCORE in sft_sysucc_2023) as a polygenic risk score.

reply.answer:
No study in cBioPortal has a polygenic risk score (PRS). I searched every clinical attribute name, display name, and description across all studies for PRS, polygenic, genetic risk, and related terms, and found no match.

The closest matches are other risk scores, which are not polygenic:

- **MDS IWG 2022** (`mds_iwg_2022`): IPSS-M and IPSS-R prognostic scores (`IPSSM_SCORE`, `IPSSR_SCORE`)
- **Colon cancer, Sidra-LUMC 2023** (`coad_silu_2022`): a microbiome risk score (`MBR_SCORE`)
- **Solitary fibrous tumors, SYSUCC 2023** (`sft_sysucc_2023`): a nomogram-based total risk score (`RISK_SCORE`)

These are clinical or molecular prognostic scores, not inherited genetic risk. My search covered clinical attributes only. If a study stored a PRS as a genomic or generic-assay profile, it would not appear here, but I found no sign of one.

You can browse all studies at https://www.cbioportal.org.

# Clinical Data Query Guide

## Overview
Clinical data in cBioPortal is stored at both patient and sample levels. Understanding the distinction is crucial for accurate analysis.

## Data Organization

### Patient-Level vs Sample-Level Data
- **Patient-level**: Demographics, overall survival, disease stage (stored once per patient)
- **Sample-level**: Sample type, sequencing platform, purity (can have multiple per patient)

### Key Tables
- `clinical_patient`: Patient-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_sample`: Sample-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_data_derived`: Pre-joined view combining both levels
- `clinical_attribute_meta`: Metadata about available clinical attributes

## Recommended Approach: Use clinical_data_derived

The `clinical_data_derived` table is pre-joined and optimized for most queries:

```sql
-- Get clinical data for specific attributes
SELECT
    sample_unique_id,
    patient_unique_id,
    attribute_name,
    attribute_value
FROM clinical_data_derived
WHERE
    cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
    AND attribute_name IN ('CANCER_TYPE', 'SAMPLE_TYPE', 'TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS');
```

**Always start here** to see what clinical attributes are available for a specific study:

```sql

SELECT

question.question: What is the frequency of TP53 mutations in lung cancer?
question.notes:
A correct answer must: report a percentage (altered / mutation-profiled samples), starting from the TCGA PanCancer Atlas lung studies (LUAD, LUSC); if several studies are used, give a range per study and warn that samples can overlap between cohorts.
Must not: report raw sample counts only, average across studies, or give a frequency above 100%.

reply.answer:
TP53 is mutated in roughly half to over 80% of lung cancer samples, depending on the histology. The rate is highest in small cell lung cancer and lung squamous cell carcinoma and lowest in some lung adenocarcinoma cohorts.

Figures are sample-level (altered samples / samples profiled for TP53 × 100), since the views I used count samples rather than patients.

| Lung cancer type (study) | TP53 mutated / profiled | Frequency |
|---|---|---|
| Small cell lung cancer (sclc_ucologne_2015) | 103 / 120 | 85.8% |
| Lung squamous cell carcinoma (TCGA PanCancer Atlas, lusc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018) | 404 / 484 | 83.5% |
| Non-small cell lung cancer, MSK-IMPACT (luad_mskimpact_2021) | 93 / 141 | 66.0% |
| Lung adenocarcinoma (TCGA PanCancer Atlas, luad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018) | 295 / 566 | 52.1% |
| Non-small cell lung cancer, NCI never-smokers (lung_nci_2022) | 36 / 232 | 15.5% |

- **Pooled TCGA lung (LUAD + LUSC, labelled "Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer" in the TCGA PanCancer Atlas):** 699 / 1,050 = 66.6%.
- The NCI never-smoker cohort is a low outlier, probably reflecting its patient population.
- Each row is a different study, so I haven't pooled them into one number. Samples can overlap across cohorts.

You can view TP53 alterations across the two TCGA lung studies in the [TP53 OncoPrint for TCGA lung adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma](https://www.cbioportal.org/results/oncoprint?cancer_study_list=luad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Clusc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018&gene_list=TP53&case_set_id=all).

# Mutation Frequency Analysis Guide

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`
- For quick frequency lookups, **prefer the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas study first**, then offer to expand to other studies
- When reporting across multiple studies, show **ranges** (e.g., "TP53 is mutated in 30–60% of samples") rather than a single average
- **NEVER** sum mutation events across studies to compute an aggregate frequency — this can exceed 100% due to double-counting
- Warn users that samples may overlap across cohorts (e.g., MSK studies may share patients)
- **Choose and state the counting unit**: use patient-level frequencies for prevalence/rate questions unless the user explicitly asks for samples; use sample-level frequencies when the user asks about samples.
- **For "across cancer types" questions**, jump to the [Cross-Cancer-Type Mutation Frequency](#cross-cancer-type-mutation-frequency) section below — there is one correct recipe and several common wrong ones.

## Counting Unit: Samples vs Patients

Before answering any mutation count or frequency question, decide whether the unit is samples or patients and state that choice in the answer.

| User wording | Counting unit |
|--------------|---------------|
| "prevalence", "rate", "fraction of patients", "patients with", "how common is" | Patient-level: `COUNT(DISTINCT patient_unique_id)` |

reply.answer:
The most frequently mutated genes differ between the two main lung cancer types. I used the TCGA PanCancer Atlas studies, which give consistent, comparable counts. Frequencies are patient-level (one sample per patient in these cohorts), calculated as altered samples divided by samples profiled for that gene.

**Lung Adenocarcinoma (LUAD), TCGA PanCancer Atlas, n = 566**

| Rank | Gene | Altered / profiled | Frequency |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | TP53 | 295 / 566 | 52.1% |
| 2 | TTN | 272 / 566 | 48.1% |
| 3 | MUC16 | 242 / 566 | 42.8% |
| 4 | CSMD3 | 226 / 566 | 39.9% |
| 5 | RYR2 | 217 / 566 | 38.3% |
| 6 | LRP1B | 201 / 566 | 35.5% |
| 7 | ZFHX4 | 185 / 566 | 32.7% |
| 8 | USH2A | 177 / 566 | 31.3% |
| 9 | KRAS | 168 / 566 | 29.7% |
| 10 | XIRP2 | 150 / 566 | 26.5% |

**Lung Squamous Cell Carcinoma (LUSC), TCGA PanCancer Atlas, n = 484**

| Rank | Gene | Altered / profiled | Frequency |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | TP53 | 404 / 484 | 83.5% |
| 2 | TTN | 345 / 484 | 71.3% |
| 3 | CSMD3 | 209 / 484 | 43.2% |
| 4 | RYR2 | 192 / 484 | 39.7% |
| 5 | MUC16 | 188 / 484 | 38.8% |
| 6 | LRP1B | 171 / 484 | 35.3% |
| 7 | USH2A | 160 / 484 | 33.1% |
| 8 | SYNE1 | 151 / 484 | 31.2% |
| 9 | ZFHX4 | 143 / 484 | 29.5% |
| 10 | FAM135B | 118 / 484 | 24.4% |

KRAS is not in the LUSC top 15 in this cohort.

**Interpretation notes**
- TP53 is the most mutated gene in both types, and it is more common in LUSC (83.5%) than in LUAD (52.1%).
- TTN, MUC16, CSMD3, RYR2, and LRP1B are large genes that are frequently mutated as passengers, so their high rates do not by themselves indicate a driver role. This is a descriptive observation from the frequencies only; I did not test for significance.
- The rankings reflect the TCGA PanCancer Atlas cohorts. Other lung studies in cBioPortal (for example, MSK or CPTAC cohorts) may show different frequencies.

[View OncoPrint for TP53, TTN, MUC16, and KRAS across LUAD and LUSC](https://www.cbioportal.org/results/oncoprint?cancer_study_list=luad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Clusc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018&gene_list=TP53%0ATTN%0AMUC16%0AKRAS&case_set_id=all)

# Sample and Study Filtering Guide

## Overview
Proper filtering is essential for meaningful cBioPortal analysis. This guide covers filtering by studies, sample types, and other criteria.

## Study-Level Filtering

### 1. Always Filter by Study
Every query should specify a study to ensure consistent results:

```sql
-- Always include study filtering
SELECT *
FROM your_table
WHERE
    cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
    -- Additional filters...
```

### 2. Find Available Studies

```sql
-- Discover available studies
SELECT
    cancer_study_identifier,
    name,
    description,
    type_of_cancer_id
FROM cancer_study
ORDER BY cancer_study_identifier;
```

### 3. Study Information

```sql
-- Get detailed study information
SELECT
    cs.cancer_study_identifier,
    cs.name as study_name,
    cs.description,
    cs.sample_count,
    COUNT(DISTINCT p.internal_id) as patient_count
FROM cancer_study cs
LEFT JOIN patient p ON cs.cancer_study_id = p.cancer_study_id
WHERE
    cs.cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
GROUP BY cs.cancer_study_identifier, cs.name, cs.description, cs.sample_count;
```

### 4. Find Studies by Available Data Types

Use this when the user asks *"which studies have mutation and copy-number data for X"*, *"studies with expression for Y"*, *"is there any imaging data"*, or any *"studies with Z data"* question. `cancer_study` has one precomputed sample count per data type — filter on them. question.question: Are TP53 mutations clinically actionable?
question.notes:
A correct answer must: ground any actionability statement in OncoKB (cite the evidence level) or redirect to OncoKB, and state that cBioPortal cohort data alone does not establish clinical actionability.
Must not: give therapeutic or clinical guidance from general LLM knowledge.

reply.answer:
**Short answer:** cBioPortal can't tell you whether TP53 mutations are clinically actionable. The database has no actionability tiers, and its only driver annotations don't cover TP53 in a clinically useful way.

**What the database holds for TP53:**
- About 149,000 TP53 mutation records have no driver annotation at all.
- Only about 1,300 are labelled `Putative_Driver`, and those labels come from clonal hematopoiesis studies (`msk_ch_*`) using their own criteria ("CH-PD", "Pathogenic or Likely-Pathogenic", and similar).
- The `alteration_driver_annotation` table has OncoKB-style tier fields, but every row is empty.
- OncoKB oncogenicity and therapeutic levels are computed by the cBioPortal web app at view time and aren't stored here.

**What you can check in cBioPortal:** the OncoKB-annotated view is available in the portal's results pages with the OQL `TP53: MUT_DRIVER` (or `TP53: DRIVER`). Once you pick a study, I can generate that link. The OncoKB site itself lists the therapeutic evidence for specific alterations.

**General background (not from cBioPortal data, so verify against OncoKB or the primary literature):** TP53 is a tumor suppressor. To my knowledge, no targeted therapy is approved specifically for TP53 mutations. Some clinical trials target the TP53 pathway, for example MDM2 inhibitors in TP53 wild-type tumors. Actionability depends on the specific variant, the cancer type, and the therapy.

This is research information, not clinical advice. For any patient-level decision, please work with a clinical molecular tumor board.

# Mutation Frequency Analysis Guide

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`
- For quick frequency lookups, **prefer the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas study first**, then offer to expand to other studies
- When reporting across multiple studies, show **ranges** (e.g., "TP53 is mutated in 30–60% of samples") rather than a single average
- **NEVER** sum mutation events across studies to compute an aggregate frequency — this can exceed 100% due to double-counting
- Warn users that samples may overlap across cohorts (e.g., MSK studies may share patients)
- **Choose and state the counting unit**: use patient-level frequencies for prevalence/rate questions unless the user explicitly asks for samples; use sample-level frequencies when the user asks about samples.
- **For "across cancer types" questions**, jump to the [Cross-Cancer-Type Mutation Frequency](#cross-cancer-type-mutation-frequency) section below — there is one correct recipe and several common wrong ones.

| User wording | Counting unit |

# Gene Expression Analysis Guide

This guide covers continuous-value genomic data: gene **expression**, **copy number** values, **methylation**, and related profile types. Mutation/CNA/SV *frequency* analysis lives in `cbioportal://mutation-frequency-guide`.

## Where this data lives

Continuous per-sample-per-gene values are stored in `genetic_alteration_derived`:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| `sample_unique_id` | `<study>_<sample_stable_id>` |
| `cancer_study_identifier` | study scope |
| `hugo_gene_symbol` | gene |
| `profile_type` | which assay/normalization (see below) |
| `alteration_value` | the actual value — stored as Nullable(String); cast with `toFloat64OrNull` |

`alteration_value` is a string because the same column hosts many different value scales. The `''` and `'NA'` sentinels mean "missing"; always filter them out and use `toFloat64OrNull(alteration_value) IS NOT NULL` for downstream math.

## Discovering profile types for a study

Different studies expose different profile types depending on what assays were run and how the data was normalized. Always check what a specific study supports before picking one:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT profile_type
FROM genetic_alteration_derived
WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'brca_metabric'
ORDER BY profile_type;

reply.answer:
I couldn't find a Minerva viewer link for the OHSU HTAN sample in this database, so I can't give you one.

**What I checked**
- The OHSU HTAN study here is **Breast Cancer (HTAN, 2022)**, `brca_hta9_htan_2022`. It has one patient (HTA9_1) and six samples: four metastatic biopsies, one primary, and one further primary-tumor sample. The OHSU atlas code is hta9.

- The external-resource tables hold no imaging links for this study at the sample, patient, or study level. The only patient-level link for this study is a figure from a bioRxiv preprint, not an imaging viewer.
- The other HTAN studies, MSK (`crc_hta8_htan_2024`) and Vanderbilt (`crc_hta11_htan_2021`), have no Minerva links either.

**Where to look**
- The study's patient page is here: [View HTA9_1 patient summary](https://www.cbioportal.org/patient/summary?studyId=brca_hta9_htan_2022&caseId=HTA9_1)
- The HTAN Minerva imaging may be published outside cBioPortal. The HTAN data portal (data.humantumoratlas.org) is the place to check for it.

Use this guide when the user names a study, cohort, portal, or data source that may not exist in the connected cBioPortal deployment.

# Gene Expression Analysis Guide

This guide covers continuous-value genomic data: gene **expression**, **copy number** values, **methylation**, and related profile types. Mutation/CNA/SV *frequency* analysis lives in `cbioportal://mutation-frequency-guide`.

## Where this data lives

Continuous per-sample-per-gene values are stored in `genetic_alteration_derived`:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| `sample_unique_id` | `<study>_<sample_stable_id>` |
| `cancer_study_identifier` | study scope |
| `hugo_gene_symbol` | gene |
| `profile_type` | which assay/normalization (see below) |
| `alteration_value` | the actual value — stored as Nullable(String); cast with `toFloat64OrNull` |

`alteration_value` is a string because the same column hosts many different value scales. The `''` and `'NA'` sentinels mean "missing"; always filter them out and use `toFloat64OrNull(alteration_value) IS NOT NULL` for downstream math.

## Discovering profile types for a study

Different studies expose different profile types depending on what assays were run and how the data was normalized. Always check what a specific study supports before picking one:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT profile_type
FROM genetic_alteration_derived
WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'brca_metabric'
ORDER BY profile_type;
```

Common values across the public portal:

Statistical Test Selection Guide
================================

Purpose
-------
This guide ensures the correct statistical test is selected before performing any group comparison, matching cBioPortal's own Group Comparison defaults.

HARD RULES — NEVER FABRICATE A STATISTIC
----------------------------------------
ClickHouse cannot run statistical tests. The agent therefore must NEVER produce a derived statistic that is not a literal column value from a SQL result. Specifically:

1. **Never invent a p-value.** Not "p < 0.001", not "p ≈ 0.05", not any p-value. If the user asks "what is the p-value?", the answer is *"I can't compute that — here is the 2x2 contingency table (or group statistics). Run it in cBioPortal's Group Comparison tab, in R with `fisher.test(...)` / `wilcox.test(...)`, or in Python with `scipy.stats.fisher_exact(...)` / `mannwhitneyu(...)`."*
2. **Never claim mutual exclusivity (or co-occurrence) from a contingency table alone.** A 2x2 table is not a test. question.question: what's the best way to put clinical data into cbioportal?
question.notes:
A correct answer must: describe the options: submitting to the public portal (curation team, cBioPortal/datahub, file formats), running a private instance, and visualizing own data without submission (OncoPrinter, MutationMapper); ask which use case applies.
Must not: say it cannot help.

reply.answer:
The best route depends on whether you're loading into a local cBioPortal instance or submitting a study for the public portal. In both cases the work is in the file format, and the import tooling validates it.

**1. Prepare the clinical files**

A study needs two clinical files, one per level:
- `data_clinical_patient.txt`: one row per patient (e.g., `SEX`, `AGE`, `OS_MONTHS`, `OS_STATUS`).
- `data_clinical_sample.txt`: one row per sample (e.g., `ONCOTREE_CODE`, `SAMPLE_TYPE`), with `PATIENT_ID` linking back to the patient file.

Each file starts with four header lines, followed by a column-name line and then the data:

```
#Patient Identifier	Sex	Overall Survival (Months)	Overall Survival Status
#Patient identifier	Sex of the patient	Overall survival in months	Overall survival status
#STRING	STRING	NUMBER	STRING
#1	1	1	1
PATIENT_ID	SEX	OS_MONTHS	OS_STATUS
P001	Female	34.2	0:LIVING
```

The `#datatype` line must be `STRING`, `NUMBER`, or `BOOLEAN`. Use tab-separated values and no spaces in the column names.

**2. Add a meta file for each data file**

`meta_clinical_patient.txt` and `meta_clinical_sample.txt` tell the importer what each file is:

```
cancer_study_identifier: my_study_2026
genetic_alteration_type: CLINICAL
datatype: PATIENT_ATTRIBUTES
data_filename: data_clinical_patient.txt
```

Use `SAMPLE_ATTRIBUTES` for the sample file.

**3. Follow the conventions that matter most**
- Use the standard attribute names where they exist (e.g., `OS_MONTHS`/`OS_STATUS`, `DFS_MONTHS`/`DFS_STATUS`, `AGE`, `SEX`). Standard names let the portal's survival and clinical views work automatically.
- Survival status uses the `0:LIVING` / `1:DECEASED` style, not free text.
- Cancer type should be an OncoTree code in `ONCOTREE_CODE`. Look codes up with the OncoTree site or the search tool here.
- Sample and patient IDs must match exactly across the clinical files and any mutation or CNA files.
- De-identify ages and dates before loading, and check the portal's own guidance on what is allowed.

**4. Validate and import**

- **Local instance:** Run the cBioPortal importer on the study folder. Its validator reports format and ID-matching errors before anything loads. The `cbioportal` GitHub documentation covers the exact command for your version (Docker or the Java/Perl importer).
- **Public portal:** Studies are submitted through the cBioPortal data hub on GitHub (a pull request with the files and meta files) and go through the same validation.

**For MSK:** If the data is internal, check with the MSK cBioPortal team about the institutional ingestion path before loading anything, because data-sharing and de-identification rules may apply.

If you tell me what the clinical data looks like (columns, whether it's patient- or sample-level, and whether it's for a local instance or the public portal), I can help draft the two data files and meta files.

grade.rationale: The answer provides detailed guidance on submitting clinical data to cBioPortal, covering both local instances and the public portal (via GitHub datahub), and asks which use case applies at the end. However, it omits mentioning OncoPrinter and MutationMapper as options for visualizing one's own data without full submission, which is a required element per the notes. The answer does not incorrectly decline or say it cannot help.

question.notes:
A correct answer must: use a pan-glioma cohort (e.g. lgggbm_tcga_pub) or clearly label a narrower cohort; use current OncoTree codes (GB, not the deprecated GBM) and note that glioblastoma is IDH-wildtype by definition. (Also covers cbioportal-mcp#36.)
