reply.answer:
## Mutation frequency by tumor sidedness in colorectal cancer

Across four colorectal cohorts that record sidedness, several genes show a consistent pattern. Right-sided tumors have a higher observed frequency of BRAF, PIK3CA, KRAS, SMAD4, FBXW7, PTEN, and ATM mutations, while left-sided tumors have a higher frequency of TP53 and APC mutations. These are descriptive counts. I did not run significance tests, so treat the differences as hypotheses to test.

**Method:** Each study is reported separately because the sidedness fields and cohorts differ. Frequencies are sample-level: altered samples ÷ samples profiled for that gene, excluding UNCALLED and off-panel mutations. Tumors coded as neither left nor right (e.g., transverse) were excluded.

| Gene | TCGA Nature 2012 (`coadread_tcga_pub`) L / R | MSK 2017 (`crc_msk_2017`) L / R | MSK APC-IMPACT 2020 (`crc_apc_impact_2020`) L / R | SYSUCC 2022 (`crc_sysucc_2022`) L / R |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TP53 | **63.5%** (47/74) / 34.8% (23/66) | **79.2%** (616/778) / 58.8% (201/342) | **75.6%** (146/193) / 65.1% (99/152) | **48.2%** (335/695) / 38.4% (123/320) |
| APC | **79.7%** / 63.6% | **81.6%** / 65.2% | **71.5%** / 63.8% | **46.8%** / 39.4% |
| BRAF | 1.4% (1/74) / **24.2%** (16/66) | 6.9% (54/778) / **22.8%** (78/342) | 10.9% (21/193) / **20.4%** (31/152) | 2.4% (17/695) / **8.1%** (26/320) |
| PIK3CA | 10.8% / **27.3%** | 15.9% / **29.5%** | 18.1% / **23.7%** | 7.9% / **23.4%** |
| KRAS | 28.4% / **45.5%** | 37.7% / **56.7%** | 40.9% / **60.5%** | 21.6% / **27.8%** |
| SMAD4 | 8.1% / **15.2%** | 12.9% / **20.5%** | 15.0% / **17.1%** | 6.3% / **10.9%** |
| FBXW7 | 12.2% / **22.7%** | 11.7% / **15.5%** | 7.3% / **13.2%** | 11.4% / **13.1%** |
| PTEN | 2.7% / 3.0% | 3.6% / **11.4%** | 4.1% / **8.6%** | 2.3% / **9.7%** |
| ATM | 8.1% / **21.2%** | 5.3% / **12.9%** | 5.7% / **7.9%** | 4.3% / **10.3%** |
| NRAS | 10.8% / 7.6% | 4.0% / 4.4% | 3.1% / 2.6% | 2.6% / 1.9% |

Bold marks the higher value in each row. Counts for the other studies are in parentheses where shown. NRAS shows no consistent difference.

**Patterns:**
- **BRAF** is the clearest signal. Right-sided tumors have roughly 3–10 times the frequency of left-sided tumors in every cohort.
- **TP53 and APC** are higher on the left in all four cohorts.
- **KRAS, PIK3CA, and SMAD4** are higher on the right in all four cohorts.

**Caveats:**
- The sidedness definition varies by study, and the cohorts are heterogeneous. The MSK cohorts are metastatic or mixed-stage, and TCGA is primary tumors. Pooling across studies would risk double-counting overlapping MSK patients, so I did not combine them.
- Sample-level counts were used. These cohorts are mostly one sample per patient, but I did not check this explicitly.
- `crc_msk_2026` (the largest colorectal study) and the TCGA PanCancer Atlas colorectal study do not have a sidedness field in the database, so they are not included.

To test these differences formally, the Group Comparison page for the MSK 2017 cohort compares left- and right-sided tumors using the mutations view:

[Compare Left-sided vs Right-sided tumors (MSK 2017, mutations)](https://www.cbioportal.org/comparison/mutations?comparisonId=6ad05340c2115c492d888364)

The study summary is also available at [Metastatic Colorectal Cancer (MSK, Cancer Cell 2018)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=crc_msk_2017).

# Mutation Frequency Analysis Guide

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`
- For quick frequency lookups, **prefer the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas study first**, then offer to expand to other studies
- When reporting across multiple studies, show **ranges** (e.g., "TP53 is mutated in 30–60% of samples") rather than a single average
- **NEVER** sum mutation events across studies to compute an aggregate frequency — this can exceed 100% due to double-counting
- Warn users that samples may overlap across cohorts (e.g., MSK studies may share patients)
- **Choose and state the counting unit**: use patient-level frequencies for prevalence/rate questions unless the user explicitly asks for samples; use sample-level frequencies when the user asks about samples.

# Clinical Data Query Guide

## Overview
Clinical data in cBioPortal is stored at both patient and sample levels. Understanding the distinction is crucial for accurate analysis.

## Data Organization

### Patient-Level vs Sample-Level Data
- **Patient-level**: Demographics, overall survival, disease stage (stored once per patient)
- **Sample-level**: Sample type, sequencing platform, purity (can have multiple per patient)

### Key Tables
- `clinical_patient`: Patient-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_sample`: Sample-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_data_derived`: Pre-joined view combining both levels
- `clinical_attribute_meta`: Metadata about available clinical attributes

## Recommended Approach: Use clinical_data_derived

The `clinical_data_derived` table is pre-joined and optimized for most queries:

```sql
-- Get clinical data for specific attributes
SELECT
    sample_unique_id,
    patient_unique_id,
    attribute_name,
    attribute_value
FROM clinical_data_derived

```

Statistical Test Selection Guide
================================

Purpose
-------
This guide ensures the correct statistical test is selected before performing any group comparison, matching cBioPortal's own Group Comparison defaults.

HARD RULES — NEVER FABRICATE A STATISTIC
----------------------------------------
ClickHouse cannot run statistical tests. The agent therefore must NEVER produce a derived statistic that is not a literal column value from a SQL result. Specifically:

1. **Never invent a p-value.** Not "p < 0.001", not "p ≈ 0.05", not any p-value. If the user asks "what is the p-value?", the answer is *"I can't compute that — here is the 2x2 contingency table (or group statistics). Run it in cBioPortal's Group Comparison tab, in R with `fisher.test(...)` / `wilcox.test(...)`, or in Python with `scipy.stats.fisher_exact(...)` / `mannwhitneyu(...)`."*
2. **Never claim mutual exclusivity (or co-occurrence) from a contingency table alone.** A 2x2 table is not a test. {"query": "WITH
side AS (
    SELECT cancer_study_identifier, patient_unique_id,
        any(multiIf(lower(attribute_value) LIKE '%left%', 'Left',
                    lower(attribute_value) LIKE '%right%', 'Right', 'Other')) AS sidedness
    FROM clinical_data_derived
    WHERE (cancer_study_identifier IN ('crc_sysucc_2022', 'crc_msk_2017') AND attribute_name = 'PRIMARY_TUMOR_LOCATION')
       OR (cancer_study_identifier = 'crc_apc_impact_2020' AND attribute_name = 'TUMOR_LOCATION')
       OR (cancer_study_identifier = 'coadread_tcga_pub' AND attribute_name = 'PRIMARY_SITE')
    GROUP BY cancer_study_identifier, patient_unique_id
),
samp AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT cancer_study_identifier, sample_unique_id, patient_unique_id
    FROM clinical_data_derived
    WHERE cancer_study_identifier IN ('crc_sysucc_2022', 'crc_msk_2017', 'crc_apc_impact_2020', 'coadread_tcga_pub')
      AND sample_unique_id != ''
),
sside AS (
    SELECT s.cancer_study_identifier, s.sample_unique_id, d.sidedness
    FROM samp s
    INNER JOIN side d ON d.cancer_study_identifier = s.cancer_study_identifier AND d.patient_unique_id = s.patient_unique_id
    WHERE d.sidedness IN ('Left', 'Right')
),
prof AS (

# Sample and Study Filtering Guide

## Overview
Proper filtering is essential for meaningful cBioPortal analysis. This guide covers filtering by studies, sample types, and other criteria.

## Study-Level Filtering

### 1. Always Filter by Study
Every query should specify a study to ensure consistent results:

```sql
-- Always include study filtering
SELECT *
FROM your_table
WHERE
    cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
    -- Additional filters...
```

### 2. Find Available Studies

```sql
-- Discover available studies
SELECT
    cancer_study_identifier,
    name,
    description,
    type_of_cancer_id
FROM cancer_study
ORDER BY cancer_study_identifier;
```

### 3. Study Information

```sql
-- Get detailed study information
SELECT
    cs.cancer_study_identifier,
    cs.name as study_name,
    cs.description,
    cs.sample_count,
    COUNT(DISTINCT p.internal_id) as patient_count
FROM cancer_study cs
LEFT JOIN patient p ON cs.cancer_study_id = p.cancer_study_id
WHERE
    cs.cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
GROUP BY cs.cancer_study_identifier, cs.name, cs.description, cs.sample_count;
```

# Clinical Data Query Guide

## Overview
Clinical data in cBioPortal is stored at both patient and sample levels. Understanding the distinction is crucial for accurate analysis.

## Data Organization

### Patient-Level vs Sample-Level Data
- **Patient-level**: Demographics, overall survival, disease stage (stored once per patient)
- **Sample-level**: Sample type, sequencing platform, purity (can have multiple per patient)

### Key Tables
- `clinical_patient`: Patient-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_sample`: Sample-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_data_derived`: Pre-joined view combining both levels
- `clinical_attribute_meta`: Metadata about available clinical attributes

## Recommended Approach: Use clinical_data_derived

The `clinical_data_derived` table is pre-joined and optimized for most queries:

```sql
-- Get clinical data for specific attributes
SELECT
    sample_unique_id,
    patient_unique_id,
    attribute_name,
    attribute_value
FROM clinical_data_derived
WHERE
    cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
    AND attribute_name IN ('CANCER_TYPE', 'SAMPLE_TYPE', 'TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS');
```

Statistical Test Selection Guide
================================

Purpose
-------
This guide ensures the correct statistical test is selected before performing any group comparison, matching cBioPortal's own Group Comparison defaults.

HARD RULES — NEVER FABRICATE A STATISTIC
----------------------------------------
ClickHouse cannot run statistical tests. The agent therefore must NEVER produce a derived statistic that is not a literal column value from a SQL result. Specifically:

1. **Never invent a p-value.** Not "p < 0.001", not "p ≈ 0.05", not any p-value. If the user asks "what is the p-value?", the answer is *"I can't compute that — here is the 2x2 contingency table (or group statistics). Run it in cBioPortal's Group Comparison tab, in R with `fisher.test(...)` / `wilcox.test(...)`, or in Python with `scipy.stats.fisher_exact(...)` / `mannwhitneyu(...)`."*
2. **Never claim mutual exclusivity (or co-occurrence) from a contingency table alone.** A 2x2 table is not a test. The shape "altered/not altered × group A/group B" needs Fisher's exact + a defined direction (odds ratio < 1 with significant p). Without that test, the agent presents the table and stops. Descriptive phrasing is also a claim: "largely/mostly mutually exclusive", "rarely co-occur", "tend to co-occur" are forbidden without the test — point to cBioPortal's Mutual Exclusivity tab instead.
3. **Never report a "median" that came from `AVG(...)` or any non-median aggregate.** "Median" and "mean" are differen … (11484 more chars)

graded.question: Are there DNA methylation differences between lower grade glioma molecular subtypes?
graded.notes:
A correct answer must: link to the group comparison DNA methylation tab (probe-level, e.g. cg00000292). (Rephrased from follow-ups.)

question.question: In lower grade glioma, are there genes which are overexpressed in any of the molecular subtypes?
question.notes:
A correct answer must: use an LGG study that has mRNA expression data (e.g. lgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018) and link to the group comparison mRNA tab. (Rephrased from a follow-up in an LGG molecular-subtype conversation.)
Must not: link to the mRNA tab of a study without expression data (e.g. lgggbm_tcga_pub).

reply.answer:
In the TCGA lower-grade glioma cohort, all three molecular subtypes have genes that are clearly higher than in the other two. The strongest signal is in IDH-wildtype tumors.

**Data used:** TCGA Brain Lower Grade Glioma (PanCancer Atlas, `lgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018`), 507 patients with a SUBTYPE call (IDH-wildtype 92; IDH-mutant 1p/19q-codeleted 167; IDH-mutant non-codeleted 248). Values are mean mRNA expression (RSEM, log2 scale) per subtype, compared with the higher of the other two subtypes. These are descriptive differences, not statistical tests.

**IDH-wildtype (higher than both IDH-mutant groups)**
- CHI3L1: 13.7 vs ~7.6 (+5.9)
- AQP5: +5.2
- POSTN: +5.0
- MOXD1: +4.9
- MEOX2: +4.5
- LTF: +4.4
- Also notable: TIMP1 (+3.8), IGFBP2 (+3.7), PDPN (+3.6), SERPINA5 (+3.5), IL13RA2 (+3.3)

**IDH-mutant, 1p/19q-codeleted (higher than both other subtypes)**
- TRIM67: +4.5 (highest expression in this subtype, 11.2)
- TLX1: +3.4
- LHX5: +3.3
- MARCHF4: +3.0
- L1CAM: +3.0
- SLC17A8: +3.0
- MSX2: +2.8
- CACNG2: +2.8
- Also notable: GRIN3A, SYT4, SVOP, MYT1L, GABRG2, KCNK3, CHGB, KCNJ11

**IDH-mutant, non-codeleted (higher than both other subtypes)**
- TPTEP1: +4.2
- ZNF560: +2.9
- REM1: +2.5
- CHST9: +2.2
- IRX1: +2.2
- C1QL4: +2.1
- IRX2: +2.0
- MSTN: +2.0
- Fewer genes pass the same threshold here than in the other two subtypes.

**Caveats**
- Only genes with a difference of at least 1 log2 unit are listed, and the top 40 per subtype are shown. This is a sorted scan, not a significance test. No p-values were computed; those need to be run in cBioPortal or in R/Python.
- Using within-study z-scores instead of raw expression gives a similar picture for the codeleted group but a weaker one for the other two, so the ranking depends on the scale used.
- I checked only the TCGA PanCancer Atlas study. Other lower-grade glioma studies in cBioPortal (for example `difg_glass_2019` and `glioma_mskcc_2019`) may show different results.

To view the expression comparison for all genes across the three subtypes in cBioPortal, use the [mRNA Group Comparison for LGG subtypes](https://www.cbioportal.org/comparison/mrna?comparisonId=6ab5c836c2115c492d884e03).

tool_calls.name: read_guide
tool_calls.result:
# Gene Expression Analysis Guide

This guide covers continuous-value genomic data: gene **expression**, **copy number** values, **methylation**, and related profile types. Mutation/CNA/SV *frequency* analysis lives in `cbioportal://mutation-frequency-guide`.

## Where this data lives

Continuous per-sample-per-gene values are stored in `genetic_alteration_derived`:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| `sample_unique_id` | `<study>_<sample_stable_id>` |
| `cancer_study_identifier` | study scope |
| `hugo_gene_symbol` | gene |
| `profile_type` | which assay/normalization (see below) |
| `alteration_value` | the actual value — stored as Nullable(String); cast with `toFloat64OrNull` |

question.question: What are the frequencies of different KRAS mutations in TCGA PanCan Lung Adenocarcinoma?
question.notes:

Must not: link to OncoPrint and explain how to navigate to Mutations, or add "what you'll find" summaries from background knowledge.

reply.answer:
In TCGA PanCancer Atlas Lung Adenocarcinoma (`luad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018`), KRAS is mutated in **168 of 566 profiled samples (29.7%)**. Because this study has one sample per patient, these counts are also patient counts.

Frequencies below use 566 profiled samples as the denominator.

| KRAS variant | Mutation type | Samples | % of 566 |
|---|---|---|---|
| G12C | Missense | 70 | 12.4% |
| G12V | Missense | 40 | 7.1% |
| G12D | Missense | 20 | 3.5% |
| G12A | Missense | 17 | 3.0% |
| G13C | Missense | 7 | 1.2% |
| G12S | Missense | 5 | 0.9% |
| G13D | Missense | 3 | 0.5% |
| L19F | Missense | 3 | 0.5% |
| Q61L | Missense | 3 | 0.5% |
| A146P | Missense | 1 | 0.2% |
| D33E | Missense | 1 | 0.2% |
| K88* | Nonsense | 1 | 0.2% |
| Q61H | Missense | 1 | 0.2% |

The variant rows add up to 172 because a few samples carry two KRAS mutations, so the per-variant rows overcount the 168 unique samples. G12 substitutions dominate, and G12C is the most common single variant.

Explore the individual mutations in the cBioPortal [KRAS mutations view for this study](https://www.cbioportal.org/results/mutations?cancer_study_list=luad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018&gene_list=KRAS%3A+MUT&case_set_id=luad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018_all).

# Gene Expression Analysis Guide

This guide covers continuous-value genomic data: gene **expression**, **copy number** values, **methylation**, and related profile types. Mutation/CNA/SV *frequency* analysis lives in `cbioportal://mutation-frequency-guide`.

## Where this data lives

Continuous per-sample-per-gene values are stored in `genetic_alteration_derived`:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| `sample_unique_id` | `<study>_<sample_stable_id>` |
| `cancer_study_identifier` | study scope |

Different studies expose different profile types depending on what assays were run and how the data was normalized. Always check what a specific study supports before picking one:

```sql
FROM genetic_alteration_derived
```

Statistical Test Selection Guide
================================

Purpose
-------
This guide ensures the correct statistical test is selected before performing any group comparison, matching cBioPortal's own Group Comparison defaults.

HARD RULES — NEVER FABRICATE A STATISTIC
----------------------------------------
ClickHouse cannot run statistical tests. The agent therefore must NEVER produce a derived statistic that is not a literal column value from a SQL result. Specifically:

1. **Never invent a p-value.** Not "p < 0.001", not "p ≈ 0.05", not any p-value. If the user asks "what is the p-value?", the answer is *"I can't compute that — here is the 2x2 contingency table (or group statistics). Run it in cBioPortal's Group Comparison tab, in R with `fisher.test(...)` / `wilcox.test(...)`, or in Python with `scipy.stats.fisher_exact(...)` / `mannwhitneyu(...)`."*
2. **Never claim mutual exclusivity (or co-occurrence) from a contingency table alone.** A 2x2 table is not a test. # Clinical Data Query Guide

## Overview
Clinical data in cBioPortal is stored at both patient and sample levels. Understanding the distinction is crucial for accurate analysis.

## Data Organization

### Patient-Level vs Sample-Level Data
- **Patient-level**: Demographics, overall survival, disease stage (stored once per patient)
- **Sample-level**: Sample type, sequencing platform, purity (can have multiple per patient)

### Key Tables
- `clinical_patient`: Patient-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_sample`: Sample-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_data_derived`: Pre-joined view combining both levels
- `clinical_attribute_meta`: Metadata about available clinical attributes

## Recommended Approach: Use clinical_data_derived

The `clinical_data_derived` table is pre-joined and optimized for most queries:

# Sample and Study Filtering Guide

## Overview
Proper filtering is essential for meaningful cBioPortal analysis. This guide covers filtering by studies, sample types, and other criteria.

## Study-Level Filtering

### 1. Always Filter by Study
Every query should specify a study to ensure consistent results:

```sql
-- Always include study filtering
SELECT *
FROM your_table
WHERE
    cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
    -- Additional filters...
```

### 2. Find Available Studies

```sql
-- Discover available studies
SELECT
    cancer_study_identifier,
    name,
    description,
    type_of_cancer_id
FROM cancer_study
ORDER BY cancer_study_identifier;
```

### 3. Study Information

```sql
-- Get detailed study information
SELECT
    cs.cancer_study_identifier,
    cs.name as study_name,
    cs.description,
    cs.sample_count,
    COUNT(DISTINCT p.internal_id) as patient_count
FROM cancer_study cs
LEFT JOIN patient p ON cs.cancer_study_id = p.cancer_study_id
WHERE
    cs.cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
GROUP BY cs.cancer_study_identifier, cs.name, cs.description, cs.sample_count;
```

# Gene Resolution Guide

Use this guide before querying gene expression, mutation, copy-number, methylation, or structural-variant data when the user's gene term may be ambiguous.

## Routing Triggers

Read this guide when the user mentions:

- a gene family shorthand: `CD3`, `HLA`, `KRT`, `MUC`, `MT-`, `IGH`, `IGK`, `IGL`
- a marker name that may refer to multiple genes or proteins
- a gene alias, old symbol, or informal name
- a wildcard-like term such as "all CD3 genes"

These examples are not exhaustive. Apply this guide to any gene term that may resolve to multiple symbols, aliases, paralogs, family members, or marker genes.

## Core Rule

Do not silently aggregate multiple genes when the user names an ambiguous symbol. Either ask for clarification or choose a clearly standard marker and state the choice.

For example, "CD3 expression" can refer to `CD3D`, `CD3E`, or `CD3G`; in many immune-marker contexts `CD3E` is the standard marker, but the agent must not average all CD3 genes unless the user asks for a combined signature.

## Gene Discovery Query

After validating the gene table exists, search exact symbols first, then prefix/alias-like matches:

```sql
SELECT
    hugo_gene_symbol,
    entrez_gene_id
FROM gene
WHERE upper(hugo_gene_symbol) = upper('CD3')
   OR upper(hugo_gene_symbol) LIKE upper('CD3%')
ORDER BY hugo_gene_symbol
LIMIT 50;
```

This guide covers continuous-value genomic data: gene **expression**, **copy number** values, **methylation**, and related profile types. Mutation/CNA/SV *frequency* analysis lives in `cbioportal://mutation-frequency-guide`.

| Column | Description |
|---|---|

# Sample and Study Filtering Guide

## Overview
Proper filtering is essential for meaningful cBioPortal analysis. This guide covers filtering by studies, sample types, and other criteria.

## Study-Level Filtering

### 1. Always Filter by Study
Every query should specify a study to ensure consistent results:

```sql
-- Always include study filtering
SELECT *
FROM your_table
WHERE
    cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
    -- Additional filters...
```

### 2. Find Available Studies

```sql
-- Discover available studies
SELECT
    cancer_study_identifier,
    name,
    description,
    type_of_cancer_id
FROM cancer_study
ORDER BY cancer_study_identifier;
```

### 3. Study Information

```sql
-- Get detailed study information
SELECT
    cs.cancer_study_identifier,
    cs.name as study_name,
    cs.description,
    cs.sample_count,
    COUNT(DISTINCT p.internal_id) as patient_count
FROM cancer_study cs
LEFT JOIN patient p ON cs.cancer_study_id = p.cancer_study_id
WHERE
    cs.cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
GROUP BY cs.cancer_study_identifier, cs.name, cs.description, cs.sample_count;
```

### 4. Find Studies by Available Data Types

Use this when the user asks *"which studies have mutation and copy-number data for X"*, *"studies with expression for Y"*, *"is there any imaging data"*, or any *"studies with Z data"* question. `cancer_study` has one precomputed sample count per data type — filter on them. Statistical Test Selection Guide
================================

Purpose
-------
This guide ensures the correct statistical test is selected before performing any group comparison, matching cBioPortal's own Group Comparison defaults.

HARD RULES — NEVER FABRICATE A STATISTIC
----------------------------------------
ClickHouse cannot run statistical tests. The agent therefore must NEVER produce a derived statistic that is not a literal column value from a SQL result. Specifically:

1. **Never invent a p-value.** Not "p < 0.001", not "p ≈ 0.05", not any p-value. If the user asks "what is the p-value?", the answer is *"I can't compute that — here is the 2x2 contingency table (or group statistics). Run it in cBioPortal's Group Comparison tab, in R with `fisher.test(...)` / `wilcox.test(...)`, or in Python with `scipy.stats.fisher_exact(...)` / `mannwhitneyu(...)`."*
2. **Never claim mutual exclusivity (or co-occurrence) from a contingency table alone.** A 2x2 table is not a test. The shape "altered/not altered × group A/group B" needs Fisher's exact + a defined direction (odds ratio < 1 with significant p). Without that test, the agent presents the table and stops. # Mutation Frequency Analysis Guide

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`
- For quick frequency lookups, **prefer the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas study first**, then offer to expand to other studies
- When reporting across multiple studies, show **ranges** (e.g., "TP53 is mutated in 30–60% of samples") rather than a single average
- **NEVER** sum mutation events across studies to compute an aggregate frequency — this can exceed 100% due to double-counting
- Warn users that samples may overlap across cohorts (e.g., MSK studies may share patients)

# Gene Expression Analysis Guide

This guide covers continuous-value genomic data: gene **expression**, **copy number** values, **methylation**, and related profile types. Mutation/CNA/SV *frequency* analysis lives in `cbioportal://mutation-frequency-guide`.

## Where this data lives

Continuous per-sample-per-gene values are stored in `genetic_alteration_derived`:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| `sample_unique_id` | `<study>_<sample_stable_id>` |
| `cancer_study_identifier` | study scope |
| `hugo_gene_symbol` | gene |
| `profile_type` | which assay/normalization (see below) |
| `alteration_value` | the actual value — stored as Nullable(String); cast with `toFloat64OrNull` |

`alteration_value` is a string because the same column hosts many different value scales. The `''` and `'NA'` sentinels mean "missing"; always filter them out and use `toFloat64OrNull(alteration_value) IS NOT NULL` for downstream math.

## Discovering profile types for a study

Different studies expose different profile types depending on what assays were run and how the data was normalized. Always check what a specific study supports before picking one:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT profile_type
FROM genetic_alteration_derived
WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'brca_metabric'
ORDER BY profile_type;
```

tool_calls.input:
{"query": "WITH cohort AS (
    SELECT cancer_study_identifier FROM cancer_study_query_preferences WHERE preference_name = 'pan_cancer_tcga'
),
ct AS (
    SELECT sample_unique_id, attribute_value AS cancer_type
    FROM clinical_data_derived
    WHERE attribute_name = 'CANCER_TYPE' AND cancer_study_identifier IN (SELECT cancer_study_identifier FROM cohort)
)
SELECT ct.cancer_type,
       count() AS samples,
       round(median(log2(toFloat64OrNull(g.alteration_value) + 1)), 2) AS median_log2_rsem,
       round(quantile(0.9)(log2(toFloat64OrNull(g.alteration_value) + 1)), 2) AS p90_log2_rsem
FROM genetic_alteration_derived g
JOIN ct USING (sample_unique_id)
WHERE g.cancer_study_identifier IN (SELECT cancer_study_identifier FROM cohort)
  AND g.hugo_gene_symbol = 'EGFR'
  AND g.profile_type = 'rna_seq_v2_mrna'
  AND g.alteration_value NOT IN ('', 'NA')
  AND toFloat64OrNull(g.alteration_value) IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY ct.cancer_type
ORDER BY median_log2_rsem DESC", "max_rows": 100}

**EGFR point mutations in lung cancer: TCGA PanCancer Atlas cohorts**

I've taken "point mutations" to mean single-residue protein changes: missense, nonsense, and splice-site/splice-region calls. In-frame insertions and deletions are excluded. Tell me if you want a different definition, such as including the in-frame indels (which are common in EGFR) or a different set of studies.

**Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), TCGA PanCancer Atlas: 566 profiled samples**
- Missense: 41 samples (53 mutation events)
- Nonsense: 2 samples
- Splice region: 1 sample
- Total point-type: about 44 samples, or 7.8%
- Most frequent protein changes: L858R (23 samples), L861Q (3), G719A, L62R, S768I, T790M (2 each). The rest are singletons.

**Lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC), TCGA PanCancer Atlas: 484 profiled samples**
- Missense: 9 samples
- Splice region: 2 samples
- Splice site: 1 sample
- Nonsense: 1 sample
- Total point-type: about 13 samples, or 2.7%
- Most frequent: L861Q (2 samples). The rest are singletons.

**Other lung cohorts (counts only, no frequency calculated)**
- Lung Adenocarcinoma (MSK, 2017; `lung_msk_2017`): missense in 140 patients. The most common changes were L858R (70 patients) and T790M (47). Pooling counts across MSK lung studies risks double-counting shared patients, so I've kept them separate.
- Lung Adenocarcinoma (MSK, 2020; `luad_mskcc_2020`): missense in 106 patients, of which L858R accounts for 82.

Notes:
- Silent (synonymous) EGFR variants do not appear in any of these studies, as is typical for public cBioPortal data.
- The TCGA counts are per sample, and the MSK counts are per patient.
- These studies have no driver annotations in the database, so I have not labelled any variant as oncogenic or a driver.

[View EGFR mutations in TCGA lung adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma](https://www.cbioportal.org/results/mutations?cancer_study_list=luad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Clusc_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018&gene_list=EGFR%3A+MUT&case_set_id=all)

# Mutation Frequency Analysis Guide

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`
- For quick frequency lookups, **prefer the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas study first**, then offer to expand to other studies
- When reporting across multiple studies, show **ranges** (e.g., "TP53 is mutated in 30–60% of samples") rather than a single average
- **NEVER** sum mutation events across studies to compute an aggregate frequency — this can exceed 100% due to double-counting
- Warn users that samples may overlap across cohorts (e.g., MSK studies may share patients)
- **Choose and state the counting unit**: use patient-level frequencies for prevalence/rate questions unless the user explicitly asks for samples; use sample-level frequencies when the user asks about samples.
- **For "across cancer types" questions**, jump to the [Cross-Cancer-Type Mutation Frequency](#cross-cancer-type-mutation-frequency) section below — there is one correct recipe and several common wrong ones.

## Counting Unit: Samples vs Patients

Before answering any mutation count or frequency question, decide whether the unit is samples or patients and state that choice in the answer.

| User wording | Counting unit |

| "prevalence", "rate", "fraction of patients", "patients with", "how common is" | Patient-level: `COUNT(DISTINCT patient_unique_id)` |

### 16. 🚨 SILENT QUERY SUBSTITUTION ("did you mean...")

When the user's wording differs from canonical terminology (e.g. "V600V" looks like "V600E" with a typo, or "point mutation" sounds like "missense"), it is forbidden to silently rewrite the question and answer the rewritten version. Doing so produces an answer that looks confident but is for a different question — the user cannot tell what was changed.

#### ❌ Wrong: silently substitute

> User: *"Find patients in colorectal cancer with the V600V alteration in BRAF"*
> Agent: *(internally treats this as V600E)* "I found 412 samples with BRAF V600E in colorectal studies..."

> User: *"What is the most prevalent TP53 mutation in uterine cancer that is not a point mutation?"*
> Agent: *(internally treats "point mutation" = "missense", silently excludes only missense)* "The most prevalent non-missense TP53 mutation is..."

For an unusual-looking variant the user may have typed deliberately:

# Gene Expression Analysis Guide

This guide covers continuous-value genomic data: gene **expression**, **copy number** values, **methylation**, and related profile types. Mutation/CNA/SV *frequency* analysis lives in `cbioportal://mutation-frequency-guide`.

## Where this data lives

Continuous per-sample-per-gene values are stored in `genetic_alteration_derived`:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| `sample_unique_id` | `<study>_<sample_stable_id>` |
| `cancer_study_identifier` | study scope |
| `hugo_gene_symbol` | gene |
| `profile_type` | which assay/normalization (see below) |
| `alteration_value` | the actual value — stored as Nullable(String); cast with `toFloat64OrNull` |

`alteration_value` is a string because the same column hosts many different value scales. The `''` and `'NA'` sentinels mean "missing"; always filter them out and use `toFloat64OrNull(alteration_value) IS NOT NULL` for downstream math.

## Discovering profile types for a study

Different studies expose different profile types depending on what assays were run and how the data was normalized. Always check what a specific study supports before picking one:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT profile_type
FROM genetic_alteration_derived
WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'brca_metabric'
ORDER BY profile_type;
```

| Family | Profile types |

# Gene Expression Analysis Guide

This guide covers continuous-value genomic data: gene **expression**, **copy number** values, **methylation**, and related profile types. Mutation/CNA/SV *frequency* analysis lives in `cbioportal://mutation-frequency-guide`.

## Where this data lives

Continuous per-sample-per-gene values are stored in `genetic_alteration_derived`:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| `sample_unique_id` | `<study>_<sample_stable_id>` |
| `cancer_study_identifier` | study scope |
| `hugo_gene_symbol` | gene |
| `profile_type` | which assay/normalization (see below) |
| `alteration_value` | the actual value — stored as Nullable(String); cast with `toFloat64OrNull` |

`alteration_value` is a string because the same column hosts many different value scales. The `''` and `'NA'` sentinels mean "missing"; always filter them out and use `toFloat64OrNull(alteration_value) IS NOT NULL` for downstream math.

## Discovering profile types for a study

Different studies expose different profile types depending on what assays were run and how the data was normalized. Always check what a specific study supports before picking one:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT profile_type
FROM genetic_alteration_derived
WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'brca_metabric'
```

Statistical Test Selection Guide
================================

Purpose
-------
This guide ensures the correct statistical test is selected before performing any group comparison, matching cBioPortal's own Group Comparison defaults.

HARD RULES — NEVER FABRICATE A STATISTIC
----------------------------------------
ClickHouse cannot run statistical tests. The agent therefore must NEVER produce a derived statistic that is not a literal column value from a SQL result. Specifically:

1. **Never invent a p-value.** Not "p < 0.001", not "p ≈ 0.05", not any p-value. If the user asks "what is the p-value?", the answer is *"I can't compute that — here is the 2x2 contingency table (or group statistics). Run it in cBioPortal's Group Comparison tab, in R with `fisher.test(...)` / `wilcox.test(...)`, or in Python with `scipy.stats.fisher_exact(...)` / `mannwhitneyu(...)`."*
2. **Never claim mutual exclusivity (or co-occurrence) from a contingency table alone.** A 2x2 table is not a test. The shape "altered/not altered × group A/group B" needs Fisher's exact + a defined direction (odds ratio < 1 with significant p). Without that test, the agent presents the table and stops. Descriptive phrasing is also a claim: "largely/mostly mutually exclusive", "rarely co-occur", "tend to co-occur" are forbidden without the test — point to cBioPortal's Mutual Exclusivity tab instead.

# Sample and Study Filtering Guide

## Overview
Proper filtering is essential for meaningful cBioPortal analysis. This guide covers filtering by studies, sample types, and other criteria.

## Study-Level Filtering

### 1. Always Filter by Study
Every query should specify a study to ensure consistent results:

```sql
-- Always include study filtering
SELECT *
FROM your_table
WHERE
    cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
    -- Additional filters...
```

### 2. Find Available Studies

```sql
-- Discover available studies
SELECT
    cancer_study_identifier,
    name,
    description,
    type_of_cancer_id
FROM cancer_study
ORDER BY cancer_study_identifier;
```

### 3. Study Information

```sql
-- Get detailed study information
SELECT
    cs.cancer_study_identifier,
    cs.name as study_name,
    cs.description,
    cs.sample_count,
    COUNT(DISTINCT p.internal_id) as patient_count
FROM cancer_study cs
LEFT JOIN patient p ON cs.cancer_study_id = p.cancer_study_id
WHERE
    cs.cancer_study_identifier = 'your_study_id'
GROUP BY cs.cancer_study_identifier, cs.name, cs.description, cs.sample_count;
```

### 4. Find Studies by Available Data Types

Use this when the user asks *"which studies have mutation and copy-number data for X"*, *"studies with expression for Y"*, *"is there any imaging data"*, or any *"studies with Z data"* question. `cancer_study` has one precomputed sample count per data type — filter on them. question.question: compare atrx mutant vs cic mutant lgg - are there different outcomes?
question.notes:
A correct answer must: build groups from mutations only (OQL `ATRX: MUT`, `CIC: MUT`, or study view mutation filters) and link to comparison/survival.

reply.answer:
**Short answer:** Crude outcomes differ. CIC-mutant tumors had fewer deaths, but that difference mostly tracks molecular subtype rather than CIC or ATRX status itself. I can't test significance here, so the survival comparison needs a Kaplan-Meier analysis.

**Study:** Brain Lower Grade Glioma (TCGA, PanCancer Atlas), `lgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018`, 514 patients. Counts are patients with overall survival data.

| Group (mutation status) | Patients | Deceased | Censored (alive at last follow-up) |
|---|---|---|---|
| ATRX mutant (CIC wild-type) | 189 | 46 (24%) | 143 |
| CIC mutant (ATRX wild-type) | 104 | 13 (13%) | 91 |
| Neither ATRX nor CIC mutant | 216 | 66 (31%) | 150 |
| Both ATRX and CIC mutant | 4 | 0 | 4 |

**Why the crude difference is mostly subtype:**
- Almost all CIC mutants (102 of 104) are IDH-mutant, 1p/19q-codeleted. Almost all ATRX mutants (183 of 189) are IDH-mutant, non-codeleted.
- Within the IDH-mutant codeleted subtype, CIC-mutant tumors died at about the same rate as the wild-type group (12/102 vs 9/62).
- The IDH-wildtype subtype has the highest death rate (46 of 85 wild-type patients). It contains only 7 ATRX mutants, so it doesn't inform the ATRX-vs-CIC comparison.
- Within IDH-mutant non-codeleted tumors, ATRX mutants had more deaths than wild-type (42/183 vs 9/62). Those wild-type numbers are small and mixed, so treat this as descriptive only.

**Survival medians:** In every group fewer than half of patients have died, so the Kaplan-Meier median is likely not reached in any of them. I haven't reported a median from raw follow-up times, because that would ignore censoring.

To see the Kaplan-Meier curves and log-rank test for the two groups:
[View ATRX mutant vs CIC mutant survival comparison](https://www.cbioportal.org/comparison/survival?comparisonId=6ab5b24fe497aad53593c238)

The comparison page shows 194 ATRX and 108 CIC patients, slightly more than above, because it doesn't require survival data to be present. To run a subtype-adjusted comparison, the Cox model would need to include subtype. That has to be done outside this database, in R or Python.

================================

Purpose
-------
This guide ensures the correct statistical test is selected before performing any group comparison, matching cBioPortal's own Group Comparison defaults.

HARD RULES — NEVER FABRICATE A STATISTIC
----------------------------------------
ClickHouse cannot run statistical tests. The agent therefore must NEVER produce a derived statistic that is not a literal column value from a SQL result. Specifically:

1. **Never invent a p-value.** Not "p < 0.001", not "p ≈ 0.05", not any p-value. If the user asks "what is the p-value?", the answer is *"I can't compute that — here is the 2x2 contingency table (or group statistics). # Clinical Data Query Guide

## Overview
Clinical data in cBioPortal is stored at both patient and sample levels. Understanding the distinction is crucial for accurate analysis.

## Data Organization

### Patient-Level vs Sample-Level Data
- **Patient-level**: Demographics, overall survival, disease stage (stored once per patient)
- **Sample-level**: Sample type, sequencing platform, purity (can have multiple per patient)

### Key Tables
- `clinical_patient`: Patient-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_sample`: Sample-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_data_derived`: Pre-joined view combining both levels
- `clinical_attribute_meta`: Metadata about available clinical attributes

## Recommended Approach: Use clinical_data_derived

The `clinical_data_derived` table is pre-joined and optimized for most queries:

```sql

FROM clinical_data_derived
```

tool_calls.input:
{"query": "WITH os AS (
  SELECT patient_unique_id,
    maxIf(toFloat64OrNull(attribute_value), attribute_name = 'OS_MONTHS') AS os_months,
    maxIf(attribute_value, attribute_name = 'OS_STATUS') AS os_status
  FROM clinical_data_derived
  WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'lgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018'
    AND attribute_name IN ('OS_MONTHS', 'OS_STATUS')
  GROUP BY patient_unique_id
),
atrx AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT patient_unique_id FROM genomic_event_derived
  WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'lgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018'
    AND variant_type = 'mutation' AND mutation_status != 'UNCALLED' AND hugo_gene_symbol = 'ATRX'
),
cic AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT patient_unique_id FROM genomic_event_derived
  WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'lgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018'
    AND variant_type = 'mutation' AND mutation_status != 'UNCALLED' AND hugo_gene_symbol = 'CIC'
)
SELECT
  patient_unique_id IN (SELECT patient_unique_id FROM atrx) AS atrx_mutant,
  patient_unique_id IN (SELECT patient_unique_id FROM cic) AS cic_mutant,
  count() AS n_patients,
  countIf(startsWith(os_status, '1')) AS n_deceased,
  countIf(startsWith(os_status, '0')) AS n_censored,
  min(os_months) AS min_followup_months,
  max(os_months) AS max_followup_months
FROM os
WHERE os_months IS NOT NULL AND os_status != ''
GROUP BY atrx_mutant, cic_mutant
ORDER BY atrx_mutant DESC, cic_mutant DESC"}

{"query": "WITH subt AS (
  SELECT patient_unique_id, anyIf(attribute_value, attribute_name = 'SUBTYPE') AS subtype
  FROM clinical_data_derived
  WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'lgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018' AND attribute_name = 'SUBTYPE'
  GROUP BY patient_unique_id
),
os AS (
  SELECT patient_unique_id,
    maxIf(toFloat64OrNull(attribute_value), attribute_name = 'OS_MONTHS') AS os_months,
    maxIf(attribute_value, attribute_name = 'OS_STATUS') AS os_status
  FROM clinical_data_derived
  WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'lgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018' AND attribute_name IN ('OS_MONTHS','OS_STATUS')
  GROUP BY patient_unique_id
),
m AS (
  SELECT patient_unique_id,
    max(hugo_gene_symbol = 'ATRX') AS atrx_mut,
    max(hugo_gene_symbol = 'CIC') AS cic_mut
  FROM genomic_event_derived
  WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'lgg_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018'
    AND variant_type = 'mutation' AND mutation_status != 'UNCALLED'
    AND hugo_gene_symbol IN ('ATRX','CIC')
  GROUP BY patient_unique_id
)
SELECT subt.subtype,
  if(m.atrx_mut = 1, 'ATRX mut', if(m.cic_mut = 1, 'CIC mut', 'ATRX/CIC wt')) AS group_name,
  count() AS n_patients,
  countIf(startsWith(os.os_status, '1')) AS n_deceased
FROM subt
JOIN os USING (patient_unique_id)
LEFT JOIN m USING (patient_unique_id)
WHERE os.os_months IS NOT NULL AND os.os_status != ''
GROUP BY subt.subtype, group_name
ORDER BY subt.subtype, group_name"}

question.question: what other genes are altered in kras mutant crc or luad
question.notes:
A correct answer must: compare KRAS-mutant vs wild-type with the wild-type group restricted to mutation-profiled samples (or use a results-view comparison).
Must not: count unprofiled samples as wild-type.

reply.answer:
**Short answer:** In TCGA PanCancer Atlas data, the most distinctive co-altered genes are **APC, PIK3CA, and BRAF in KRAS-mutant colorectal cancer**, and **TP53 and EGFR (depleted) and STK11 and ATM (enriched) in KRAS-mutant lung adenocarcinoma**. These are mutation-only comparisons of KRAS-mutant vs. KRAS wild-type samples.

**Colorectal adenocarcinoma** ([Colorectal Adenocarcinoma, TCGA PanCancer Atlas](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=coadread_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018), 594 samples)

KRAS-mutant: 218 samples profiled; KRAS wild-type: 316 samples profiled.

| Gene | KRAS-mutant | KRAS wild-type | Difference (pts) |
|---|---|---|---|
| APC | 182/218 (83.5%) | 205/316 (64.9%) | +18.6 |
| PIK3CA | 83/218 (38.1%) | 64/316 (20.3%) | +17.8 |
| PCBP1 | 20/218 (9.2%) | 5/316 (1.6%) | +7.6 |
| TMPRSS15 | 19/218 (8.7%) | 7/316 (2.2%) | +6.5 |
| BRAF | 6/218 (2.8%) | 56/316 (17.7%) | −14.9 |
| COL7A1 | 7/218 (3.2%) | 40/316 (12.7%) | −9.5 |
| ABCA13 | 22/218 (10.1%) | 55/316 (17.4%) | −7.3 |
| NRAS | 5/218 (2.3%) | 28/316 (8.9%) | −6.6 |

BRAF and NRAS are depleted in KRAS-mutant tumors, which fits the general pattern that RAS and RAF alterations rarely co-occur. Several genes at the bottom of the list (ABCA13, DOCK3, ZNF469) are large, passenger-prone genes, so their differences are less informative.

**Lung adenocarcinoma** ([Lung Adenocarcinoma, TCGA PanCancer Atlas](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=luad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018), 566 samples)

KRAS-mutant: 168 samples profiled; KRAS wild-type: 398 samples profiled.

| Gene | KRAS-mutant | KRAS wild-type | Difference (pts) |
|---|---|---|---|
| STK11 | 38/168 (22.6%) | 37/398 (9.3%) | +13.3 |
| ATM | 28/168 (16.7%) | 19/398 (4.8%) | +11.9 |
| MUC16 | 84/168 (50.0%) | 158/398 (39.7%) | +10.3 |
| CSMD1 | 48/168 (28.6%) | 77/398 (19.3%) | +9.3 |
| CNTNAP2 | 32/168 (19.0%) | 39/398 (9.8%) | +9.2 |
| TP53 | 62/168 (36.9%) | 233/398 (58.5%) | −21.6 |
| EGFR | 1/168 (0.6%) | 69/398 (17.3%) | −16.7 |
| NF1 | 8/168 (4.8%) | 58/398 (14.6%) | −9.8 |
| BRAF | 3/168 (1.8%) | 38/398 (9.5%) | −7.7 |

The strongest signals are the depletion of EGFR and TP53 and the enrichment of STK11, a pattern commonly discussed in KRAS-mutant lung cancer. The data show these co-occurrence patterns but do not establish their significance.

**Caveats**
- These are sample-level counts. Each gene's denominator is the number of samples profiled for that gene.
- These differences are descriptive. I can't compute p-values here. To test significance, use the Mutual Exclusivity or Comparison tab in cBioPortal, or Fisher's exact test in R or Python.
- The comparison uses mutations only. Copy-number changes (for example, EGFR amplification) are not included.
- Genes with fewer than 10 total mutations were excluded.

I also opened a combined OncoPrint of both studies with KRAS (mutated), APC, TP53, PIK3CA, STK11, and BRAF: [View KRAS and co-altered genes in CRC and LUAD](https://www.cbioportal.org/results/oncoprint?cancer_study_list=coadread_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018%2Cluad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018&gene_list=KRAS%3A+MUT%0AAPC%0ATP53%0APIK3CA%0ASTK11%0ABRAF&case_set_id=all)

If you want a single study, let me know which one and I can rerun the comparison with more genes.

tool_calls.result:
# Mutation Frequency Analysis Guide

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`
- For quick frequency lookups, **prefer the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas study first**, then offer to expand to other studies
- When reporting across multiple studies, show **ranges** (e.g., "TP53 is mutated in 30–60% of samples") rather than a single average
- **NEVER** sum mutation events across studies to compute an aggregate frequency — this can exceed 100% due to double-counting
- Warn users that samples may overlap across cohorts (e.g., MSK studies may share patients)
- **Choose and state the counting unit**: use patient-level frequencies for prevalence/rate questions unless the user explicitly asks for samples; use sample-level frequencies when the user asks about samples.
- **For "across cancer types" questions**, jump to the [Cross-Cancer-Type Mutation Frequency](#cross-cancer-type-mutation-frequency) section below — there is one correct recipe and several common wrong ones.

## Counting Unit: Samples vs Patients

Before answering any mutation count or frequency question, decide whether the unit is samples or patients and state that choice in the answer.

| User wording | Counting unit |
|--------------|---------------|
| "prevalence", "rate", "fraction of patients", "patients with", "how common is" | Patient-level: `COUNT(DISTINCT patient_unique_id)` |

reply.answer:
**EGFR mutations: lung vs. brain cancer**

Counts are samples, not patients. The EGFR denominator is samples profiled for EGFR, and only point mutations are counted (no amplifications or fusions).

**TCGA PanCancer Atlas (sample-level)**

| Cancer type | EGFR-mutated / profiled | % |
|---|---|---|
| Glioblastoma (brain) | 94 / 397 | 23.7% |
| Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (lung, LUAD + LUSC) | 84 / 1,050 | 8.0% |
| Lung Adenocarcinoma | 70 / 566 | 12.4% |
| Glioma (brain, lower-grade) | 35 / 514 | 6.8% |
| Lung Squamous Cell Carcinoma | 14 / 484 | 2.9% |
| Oligodendroglioma (brain) | 6 / 189 | 3.2% |

**MSK-IMPACT 50K (sample-level, panel-aware)**

| Cancer type | EGFR-mutated / profiled | % |
|---|---|---|
| Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer | 2,060 / 7,867 | 26.2% |
| Glioma | 353 / 2,322 | 15.2% |
| Small Cell Lung Cancer | 42 / 466 | 9.0% |
| Miscellaneous Brain Tumor | 3 / 58 | 5.2% |

**Takeaways**
- In both cohorts, EGFR mutation frequency is higher in brain tumors than in lung tumors when comparing the lung and brain groups in each cohort. In TCGA, glioblastoma (23.7%) is about three times the pooled NSCLC rate (8.0%). In MSK-IMPACT, NSCLC (26.2%) is higher than glioma (15.2%), so the direction depends on the cohort.
- Results differ between the two cohorts. TCGA's pooled NSCLC includes LUSC, which has a low EGFR rate, while MSK-IMPACT's NSCLC is a clinical-sequencing cohort. Treat the two sources as separate reference points, not one pooled estimate.
- These are descriptive frequencies only. I didn't run a statistical test, so I can't say whether the differences are significant. The mutation counts also aren't filtered for driver status, because these studies don't carry driver annotations.

**Interactive comparison:** [View EGFR mutations, NSCLC vs. Glioma (MSK-IMPACT 50K)](https://www.cbioportal.org/comparison/mutations?comparisonId=69f49c541c2565a03eadfc27&selectedGene=EGFR). This opens the Mutations tab with the two groups; the Survival and Clinical tabs are also available. Use the Statistics or Mutual Exclusivity tools there if you want a p-value.

Statistical Test Selection Guide
================================

Purpose
-------
This guide ensures the correct statistical test is selected before performing any group comparison, matching cBioPortal's own Group Comparison defaults.

HARD RULES — NEVER FABRICATE A STATISTIC
----------------------------------------
ClickHouse cannot run statistical tests. The agent therefore must NEVER produce a derived statistic that is not a literal column value from a SQL result. Specifically:

1. **Never invent a p-value.** Not "p < 0.001", not "p ≈ 0.05", not any p-value. If the user asks "what is the p-value?", the answer is *"I can't compute that — here is the 2x2 contingency table (or group statistics). 2. **Never claim mutual exclusivity (or co-occurrence) from a contingency table alone.** A 2x2 table is not a test. # Gene Expression Analysis Guide

This guide covers continuous-value genomic data: gene **expression**, **copy number** values, **methylation**, and related profile types. Mutation/CNA/SV *frequency* analysis lives in `cbioportal://mutation-frequency-guide`.

## Where this data lives

Continuous per-sample-per-gene values are stored in `genetic_alteration_derived`:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| `sample_unique_id` | `<study>_<sample_stable_id>` |
| `cancer_study_identifier` | study scope |
| `hugo_gene_symbol` | gene |
| `profile_type` | which assay/normalization (see below) |
| `alteration_value` | the actual value — stored as Nullable(String); cast with `toFloat64OrNull` |

`alteration_value` is a string because the same column hosts many different value scales. The `''` and `'NA'` sentinels mean "missing"; always filter them out and use `toFloat64OrNull(alteration_value) IS NOT NULL` for downstream math.

## Discovering profile types for a study

Different studies expose different profile types depending on what assays were run and how the data was normalized. Always check what a specific study supports before picking one:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT profile_type
FROM genetic_alteration_derived
```

question.question: How does overall survival compare between prostate cancer patients where TMPRSS2 is acting as the upstream donor to an ERG fusion event and patients without this fusion?
question.notes:
Group comparison links are session-based (`comparisonId` differs on every run): judge a comparison link by the groups and view the rendered page shows, not by matching the reference id or URL.
A correct answer must: use fusion-specific OQL for TMPRSS2::ERG and hand survival to Kaplan-Meier via a cBioPortal link.

reply.answer:
## TMPRSS2-ERG fusion and overall survival in prostate cancer

I could not determine from the database whether overall survival differs between TMPRSS2-ERG-positive and fusion-negative patients. The data is there, but a survival comparison needs Kaplan-Meier analysis, which the database can't run. Below are the group sizes and event counts for you to take into that analysis.

**How the groups were defined:** A patient is "fusion-positive" if a structural variant record has TMPRSS2 as the 5′ (site 1) partner and ERG as the 3′ (site 2) partner in any sample. Patients with OS_MONTHS and OS_STATUS data are included.

**Counts by prostate study (patients with OS data)**

| Study | Fusion-positive: patients / deaths | Fusion-negative: patients / deaths |
|---|---|---|
| [Prostate Cancer (MSK, 2024)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=prostate_msk_2024) | 268 / 97 | 1,933 / 819 |
| [Prostate Adenocarcinoma (MSK, Clin Cancer Res 2022)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=prad_pik3r1_msk_2021) | 226 / 91 | 1,096 / 349 |
| [Prostate Adenocarcinoma (TCGA, PanCancer Atlas)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=prad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018) | 189 / 4 | 305 / 6 |
| [Prostate Adenocarcinoma (MSK, 2025)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=prad_msk_2025) | 18 / 15 | 96 / 88 |

Smaller studies with OS data (IDH-mutant MSK 2025 and the organoid study) have only 4 fusion-positive patients each, too few to interpret. Two studies with OS data (Broad/Cornell 2013-era MCTP and SU2C 2019) recorded no TMPRSS2-ERG calls at all.

**Interpreting these numbers**
- The death counts are not a survival comparison. The two large MSK cohorts point in opposite directions when you look only at the proportion of patients who died. Event rates depend on follow-up, so only a KM analysis can say whether OS differs.
- TCGA has very few deaths (under 10 total), so it cannot support a survival comparison.
- In the MSK cohorts, the fusion-negative group may include patients who were never tested for structural variants. Only about 1,000 of 2,260 samples in the MSK 2024 study have structural variant data. A stricter comparison would limit the fusion-negative group to SV-tested patients.
- I pooled nothing across studies. Patients may overlap between the MSK cohorts, so treat each study separately.

**Next step for a survival answer:** Run Kaplan-Meier with a log-rank test in each study, for example in R:
```r
survival::survfit(Surv(OS_MONTHS, OS_STATUS == "1:DECEASED") ~ fusion, data = df)
```
You can also use the Survival tab in cBioPortal's Group Comparison for the study above. The portal's structural variant filter does not distinguish TMPRSS2-to-ERG from other fusion orientations, so you would need to define the TMPRSS2-ERG group yourself.

Statistical Test Selection Guide
================================

Purpose
-------
This guide ensures the correct statistical test is selected before performing any group comparison, matching cBioPortal's own Group Comparison defaults.

HARD RULES — NEVER FABRICATE A STATISTIC
----------------------------------------
ClickHouse cannot run statistical tests. The agent therefore must NEVER produce a derived statistic that is not a literal column value from a SQL result. Specifically:

1. **Never invent a p-value.** Not "p < 0.001", not "p ≈ 0.05", not any p-value. If the user asks "what is the p-value?", the answer is *"I can't compute that — here is the 2x2 contingency table (or group statistics). Run it in cBioPortal's Group Comparison tab, in R with `fisher.test(...)` / `wilcox.test(...)`, or in Python with `scipy.stats.fisher_exact(...)` / `mannwhitneyu(...)`."*
2. **Never claim mutual exclusivity (or co-occurrence) from a contingency table alone.** A 2x2 table is not a test. The shape "altered/not altered × group A/group B" needs Fisher's exact + a defined direction (odds ratio < 1 with significant p). Without that test, the agent presents the table and stops. Descriptive phrasing is also a claim: "largely/mostly mutually exclusive", "rarely co-occur", "tend to co-occur" are forbidden without the test — point to cBioPortal's Mutual Exclusivity tab instead.

# Clinical Data Query Guide

## Overview
Clinical data in cBioPortal is stored at both patient and sample levels. Understanding the distinction is crucial for accurate analysis.

## Data Organization

### Patient-Level vs Sample-Level Data
- **Patient-level**: Demographics, overall survival, disease stage (stored once per patient)
- **Sample-level**: Sample type, sequencing platform, purity (can have multiple per patient)

### Key Tables
- `clinical_patient`: Patient-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_sample`: Sample-level clinical attributes
- `clinical_data_derived`: Pre-joined view combining both levels
- `clinical_attribute_meta`: Metadata about available clinical attributes

reply.answer:
In the TCGA Glioblastoma Multiforme study (`gbm_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018`), counted at the patient level:

- **IDH1 R132H: 22 patients**
- **IDH1 wild-type: 366 patients**

question.question: show me all KRAS mutations in colorectal cancer that are not at position 12
question.notes:
OQL allows one `!=` exclusion per gene: `KRAS: MUT != G12` excludes every codon-12 mutation. Position ranges also work: `KRAS: MUT = (-11) MUT = (13-)`. Invalid or wrong: `!=` combined with a range, two `!=` terms on one gene, `G12*` (excludes only the nonsense change), or a `p.` prefix. Judge by what the rendered page shows.
A correct answer must: give a link whose OQL excludes codon-12 KRAS mutations in colorectal cancer (e.g. `KRAS: MUT != G12` or `KRAS: MUT = (-11) MUT = (13-)`).
Must not: emit invalid OQL or show codon-12 mutations.

reply.answer:
**KRAS mutations outside codon 12 in colorectal cancer: 77 of 534 TCGA colorectal samples (14.4%), plus 816 samples in MSK-CHORD**

I used "colorectal cancer" to mean the OncoTree colorectal types. There are two cohorts with usable data. The TCGA study is the default cohort for this kind of question. MSK-CHORD is larger, so I included it too. Counts are samples, not patients. Overlapping cohorts can double-count, so I've kept the two studies separate.

**1. TCGA Colorectal Adenocarcinoma (PanCancer Atlas), `coadread_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018`**

- Denominator: 534 samples profiled for mutations.
- Altered: 77 samples carry a non-codon-12 KRAS mutation (14.4%).

| Variant | Type | Events | Samples |
|---|---|---|---|
| G13D | Missense | 37 | 37 |
| A146T | Missense | 16 | 16 |
| K117N | Missense | 4 | 4 |
| Q61H | Missense | 4 | 4 |
| Q61K | Missense | 3 | 3 |
| G13C | Missense | 2 | 2 |
| Q61R | Missense | 2 | 2 |
| A59T, A146V, A155D, E98*, L19F, P34L, Q22K, Q61E, Q61L, Q61P, R68S, Y71C | Missense (E98* is nonsense) | 1 each | 1 each |

Four samples in this list carry more than one KRAS event. This is why the event total (81) is higher than the sample total (78).

I excluded A11_G12dup, an in-frame insertion that spans positions 11–12. It is the only variant in this list that touches codon 12. If you count it as a codon-12 change, the TCGA figure is 77 samples; if you count it as outside codon 12, it is 78.

Link: [View KRAS mutations in TCGA colorectal](https://www.cbioportal.org/results/mutations?cancer_study_list=coadread_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018&gene_list=KRAS%3A+MUT&case_set_id=coadread_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018_all). This page shows all KRAS mutations, including codon 12, so you'll need to look past those rows.

**2. MSK-CHORD (`msk_chord_2024`), samples with CANCER_TYPE = Colorectal Cancer**

- Colorectal samples in the study: 5,543.
- Samples with a non-codon-12 KRAS mutation: 816.
- I did not compute a frequency here. MSK-CHORD is panel-based, so the right denominator is the number of colorectal samples whose panel covers KRAS, which I did not calculate.

Most common variants (samples):

- G13D: 426
- A146T: 140
- Q61H: 53
- A146V: 27
- K117N: 26
- Q61K: 22
- G13C: 20
- Q61R: 15
- A59T: 13
- V14I: 10
- A146P: 9

About 50 other variants each appear in 1–7 samples.

If you want a panel-aware percentage for MSK-CHORD or a colorectal breakdown of MSK-IMPACT, I can run that next.

### 16. 🚨 SILENT QUERY SUBSTITUTION ("did you mean...")

When the user's wording differs from canonical terminology (e.g. "V600V" looks like "V600E" with a typo, or "point mutation" sounds like "missense"), it is forbidden to silently rewrite the question and answer the rewritten version. Doing so produces an answer that looks confident but is for a different question — the user cannot tell what was changed.

#### ❌ Wrong: silently substitute

> User: *"Find patients in colorectal cancer with the V600V alteration in BRAF"*
> Agent: *(internally treats this as V600E)* "I found 412 samples with BRAF V600E in colorectal studies..."

> User: *"What is the most prevalent TP53 mutation in uterine cancer that is not a point mutation?"*
> Agent: *(internally treats "point mutation" = "missense", silently excludes only missense)* "The most prevalent non-missense TP53 mutation is..."

For an unusual-looking variant the user may have typed deliberately:
- Query for what was asked, literally.
- If 0 rows come back, **explain *why* zero is the expected answer** before suggesting a likely-intended alternative. graded.question: show me all KRAS mutations in colorectal cancer that are not at position 12
graded.notes:
OQL allows one `!=` exclusion per gene: `KRAS: MUT != G12` excludes every codon-12 mutation. Position ranges also work: `KRAS: MUT = (-11) MUT = (13-)`. Invalid or wrong: `!=` combined with a range, two `!=` terms on one gene, `G12*` (excludes only the nonsense change), or a `p.` prefix. Judge by what the rendered page shows.
A correct answer must: give a link whose OQL excludes codon-12 KRAS mutations in colorectal cancer (e.g. `KRAS: MUT != G12` or `KRAS: MUT = (-11) MUT = (13-)`).
Must not: emit invalid OQL or show codon-12 mutations.

# Mutation Frequency Analysis Guide

## IMPORTANT: Reporting Mutation Frequencies
- **ALWAYS report frequencies as percentages**, not raw counts: `frequency = (altered_samples / total_profiled_samples) × 100`
- For quick frequency lookups, **prefer the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas study first**, then offer to expand to other studies
- When reporting across multiple studies, show **ranges** (e.g., "TP53 is mutated in 30–60% of samples") rather than a single average
- **NEVER** sum mutation events across studies to compute an aggregate frequency — this can exceed 100% due to double-counting
- Warn users that samples may overlap across cohorts (e.g., MSK studies may share patients)
- **Choose and state the counting unit**: use patient-level frequencies for prevalence/rate questions unless the user explicitly asks for samples; use sample-level frequencies when the user asks about samples.
- **For "across cancer types" questions**, jump to the [Cross-Cancer-Type Mutation Frequency](#cross-cancer-type-mutation-frequency) section below — there is one correct recipe and several common wrong ones.

{"query": "WITH chol AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT cancer_study_identifier, sample_unique_id
    FROM clinical_data_derived
    WHERE attribute_name = 'CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED'
      AND attribute_value IN ('Cholangiocarcinoma', 'Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma', 'Extrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma', 'Perihilar Cholangiocarcinoma')

       g.mutation_variant AS variant,
       g.mutation_type AS mutation_type,
       g.mutation_status AS status,
       count(DISTINCT g.sample_unique_id) AS samples,
       count(DISTINCT g.patient_unique_id) AS patients

  AND g.mutation_variant NOT LIKE '%R132%'
  AND (g.cancer_study_identifier, g.sample_unique_id) IN (SELECT cancer_study_identifier, sample_unique_id FROM chol)
GROUP BY study, variant, mutation_type, status
ORDER BY study, samples DESC", "max_rows": 500}

graded.question: show me cholangio with idh1 mutations other than r132
graded.notes:
OQL allows one `!=` exclusion per gene: `IDH1: MUT != R132` excludes every R132 mutation. Position ranges also work: `IDH1: MUT = (-131) MUT = (133-)`. Invalid or wrong: `!=` combined with a range, two `!=` terms on one gene, `R132*` (excludes only the nonsense change), or a `p.` prefix. Judge by what the rendered page shows.
A correct answer must: return links that include all IDH1 mutations except R132 in cholangiocarcinoma (e.g. `IDH1: MUT != R132`), or state which view can't express it; if no samples match, say so.
Must not: filter to IDH1 missense/R132 (the opposite of the request).

question.question: is there a relatinoship between mgmt methylation and idh1 mutation in glioma?
question.notes:
A correct answer must: choose a glioma study that has DNA methylation data before linking to Plots / group comparison.
Must not: link to views for a study without methylation data.

reply.answer:
**Yes, in these cBioPortal cohorts, IDH1-mutant gliomas are more often MGMT-methylated than IDH1-wildtype ones.** I did not run a significance test, so I can't give a p-value. The counts below are descriptive.

| Study | IDH1 group | MGMT methylated | MGMT unmethylated | Patients/samples with MGMT value |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Diffuse Glioma (GLASS Consortium)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=difg_glass) (samples) | IDH mutant | 89 (86%) | 14 (14%) | 103 |
| | IDH wildtype | 68 (39%) | 105 (61%) | 173 |
| [Glioma (MSK, Clin Cancer Res 2019)](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=glioma_mskcc_2019) (patients) | IDH1 mutant | 101 (56%) | 79 (44%) | 180 |
| | IDH1 wildtype | 140 (31%) | 316 (69%) | 456 |

- In the UCSF Low-Grade Glioma study ([lgg_ucsf_2014](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=lgg_ucsf_2014)), every case carries an IDH1 mutation, so there is no wildtype comparison. Of 49 cases with a known MGMT status, 38 (78%) were methylated.

**Caveats**
- MGMT status is a clinical attribute in each study, and the assay method may differ between them.
- In the MSK cohort, "wildtype" means no IDH1 mutation call. Patients without MGMT status were excluded, so the denominators are smaller than the cohort sizes.
- The GLASS and MSK rows are not pooled, because the two studies use different units (samples vs. patients).

To test the association, use Fisher's exact test on the 2×2 tables. You can run it in cBioPortal's Group Comparison tab, or in R with `fisher.test()`.

You can also browse the MSK cohort filtered to IDH1-mutant patients and check their MGMT distribution in the [Glioma (MSK, 2019) study view](https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=glioma_mskcc_2019#filterJson=%7B%22geneFilters%22%3A%5B%7B%22geneQueries%22%3A%5B%5B%7B%22hugoGeneSymbol%22%3A%22IDH1%22%7D%5D%5D%2C%22molecularProfileIds%22%3A%5B%22glioma_mskcc_2019_mutations%22%5D%7D%5D%7D).

# Gene Expression Analysis Guide

This guide covers continuous-value genomic data: gene **expression**, **copy number** values, **methylation**, and related profile types. Mutation/CNA/SV *frequency* analysis lives in `cbioportal://mutation-frequency-guide`.

## Where this data lives

Continuous per-sample-per-gene values are stored in `genetic_alteration_derived`:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| `sample_unique_id` | `<study>_<sample_stable_id>` |
| `cancer_study_identifier` | study scope |
| `hugo_gene_symbol` | gene |
| `profile_type` | which assay/normalization (see below) |
| `alteration_value` | the actual value — stored as Nullable(String); cast with `toFloat64OrNull` |

`alteration_value` is a string because the same column hosts many different value scales. The `''` and `'NA'` sentinels mean "missing"; always filter them out and use `toFloat64OrNull(alteration_value) IS NOT NULL` for downstream math.

## Discovering profile types for a study

Different studies expose different profile types depending on what assays were run and how the data was normalized. Always check what a specific study supports before picking one:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT profile_type
FROM genetic_alteration_derived
WHERE cancer_study_identifier = 'brca_metabric'
ORDER BY profile_type;
```

Common values across the public portal:

| Family | Profile types |
|---|---|
| mRNA expression | `rna_seq_v2_mrna`, `rna_seq_v2_mrna_median_Zscores`, `rna_seq_v2_mrna_median_all_sample_Zscores` (TCGA Pan … (6431 more chars)

Statistical Test Selection Guide
================================

Purpose
-------
This guide ensures the correct statistical test is selected before performing any group comparison, matching cBioPortal's own Group Comparison defaults.

HARD RULES — NEVER FABRICATE A STATISTIC
----------------------------------------
ClickHouse cannot run statistical tests. The agent therefore must NEVER produce a derived statistic that is not a literal column value from a SQL result. Specifically:

1. **Never invent a p-value.** Not "p < 0.001", not "p ≈ 0.05", not any p-value. If the user asks "what is the p-value?", the answer is *"I can't compute that — here is the 2x2 contingency table (or group statistics). Run it in cBioPortal's Group Comparison tab, in R with `fisher.test(...)` / `wilcox.test(...)`, or in Python with `scipy.stats.fisher_exact(...)` / `mannwhitneyu(...)`."*
2. **Never claim mutual exclusivity (or co-occurrence) from a contingency table alone.** A 2x2 table is not a test. # Gene Resolution Guide

Use this guide before querying gene expression, mutation, copy-number, methylation, or structural-variant data when the user's gene term may be ambiguous.

## Routing Triggers

Read this guide when the user mentions:

- a gene family shorthand: `CD3`, `HLA`, `KRT`, `MUC`, `MT-`, `IGH`, `IGK`, `IGL`
- a marker name that may refer to multiple genes or proteins
- a gene alias, old symbol, or informal name
- a wildcard-like term such as "all CD3 genes"

These examples are not exhaustive. Apply this guide to any gene term that may resolve to multiple symbols, aliases, paralogs, family members, or marker genes.

## Core Rule

Do not silently aggregate multiple genes when the user names an ambiguous symbol. Either ask for clarification or choose a clearly standard marker and state the choice.

For example, "CD3 expression" can refer to `CD3D`, `CD3E`, or `CD3G`; in many immune-marker contexts `CD3E` is the standard marker, but the agent must not average all CD3 genes unless the user asks for a combined signature.

## Gene Discovery Query

After validating the gene table exists, search exact symbols first, then prefix/alias-like matches:

```sql
SELECT

FROM gene
WHERE upper(hugo_gene_symbol) = upper('CD3')
   OR upper(hugo_gene_symbol) LIKE upper('CD3%')
ORDER BY hugo_gene_symbol
LIMIT 50;
```

question.question: show me P135L mutations in $p14^{ARF}$
question.notes:
A correct answer must: resolve p14ARF to CDKN2A (ARF isoform), keep the narrative and the link on the same cohort (pan-cancer), and say so if no samples match.

reply.answer:
**No P135L mutations are in the database for p14ARF or for CDKN2A generally.** I searched every CDKN2A mutation record for residue 135 and found only two other substitutions at that position:

| Variant | Samples | Studies |
|---|---|---|
| P135S | 8 | 7 |
| P135Q | 5 | 1 (`pancan_pdmr_2025`) |

The P135S and P135Q records are listed below. Each sample appears once.

| Study | Sample | Variant |
|---|---|---|
| ccle_broad_2019 | MEWO_SKIN | P135S |
| hnsc_tcga | TCGA-H7-8501-01 | P135S |
| mel_mskimpact_2020 | P-0001251-T01-IM3 | P135S |
| msk_impact_2017 | P-0001251-T01-IM3 | P135S |
| msk_met_2021 | P-0001251-T01-IM3 | P135S |
| msk_met_2021 | P-0015894-T01-IM6 | P135S |
| skcm_broad | MEL-JWCI-WGS-1 | P135S |
| skcm_tcga | TCGA-D3-A2JF-06 | P135S |
| pancan_pdmr_2025 | 524724-177-R-QQE (plus 4 related PDX samples) | P135Q |

Some of these samples come from overlapping MSK cohorts. For example, patient P-0001251 appears in three MSK studies, so the sample count can overcount patients.

Two points about the naming:

- **p14ARF numbering:** The database stores CDKN2A variants under one protein numbering and does not separate the p14ARF and p16INK4A isoforms. From general knowledge, not from this database, p14ARF is about 132 amino acids long, so residue 135 falls outside it. A residue-135 change would normally be reported in p16INK4A numbering. Please check the source of "P135L" before searching further.

# Gene Resolution Guide

Use this guide before querying gene expression, mutation, copy-number, methylation, or structural-variant data when the user's gene term may be ambiguous.

## Routing Triggers

Read this guide when the user mentions:

- a gene family shorthand: `CD3`, `HLA`, `KRT`, `MUC`, `MT-`, `IGH`, `IGK`, `IGL`
- a marker name that may refer to multiple genes or proteins
- a gene alias, old symbol, or informal name
- a wildcard-like term such as "all CD3 genes"

These examples are not exhaustive. Apply this guide to any gene term that may resolve to multiple symbols, aliases, paralogs, family members, or marker genes.

## Core Rule

Do not silently aggregate multiple genes when the user names an ambiguous symbol. Either ask for clarification or choose a clearly standard marker and state the choice.

For example, "CD3 expression" can refer to `CD3D`, `CD3E`, or `CD3G`; in many immune-marker contexts `CD3E` is the standard marker, but the agent must not average all CD3 genes unless the user asks for a combined signature.

## Gene Discovery Query

After validating the gene table exists, search exact symbols first, then prefix/alias-like matches:

```sql
SELECT
    hugo_gene_symbol,
    entrez_gene_id
FROM gene
WHERE upper(hugo_gene_symbol) = upper('CD3')
   OR upper(hugo_gene_symbol) LIKE upper('CD3%')
ORDER BY hugo_gene_symbol
LIMIT 50;
```

reply.answer:
**IDH1 mutation frequency in glioma, cholangiocarcinoma, and chondrosarcoma**

Source: MSK-IMPACT 50K (`msk_impact_50k_2026`), counted per sample. Denominators are samples profiled for IDH1. Each percentage is one variant's samples divided by all IDH1-profiled samples of that subtype. Multiple samples from one patient could be counted more than once.

**Glioma**

| Subtype (n profiled) | Any IDH1 mutation | R132H | R132C | R132S | R132G | R132L | Other |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant (420) | 413 (98.3%) | 352 (83.8%) | 25 (6.0%) | 17 (4.0%) | 15 (3.6%) | 3 (0.7%) | G339E 1 |
| Oligodendroglioma, IDH-mut, 1p/19q-codel (210) | 187 (89.0%) | 183 (87.1%) | 1 (0.5%) | 1 (0.5%) | 1 (0.5%) | 0 | A307V 1, R132C/S/G are single hits |
| Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype (1,543) | 8 (0.5%) | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | Eight different non-R132 variants, 1 each |

**Cholangiocarcinoma**

| Subtype (n profiled) | Any IDH1 mutation | R132C | R132L | R132G | R132S | Other |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Intrahepatic (525) | 129 (24.6%) | 94 (17.9%) | 19 (3.6%) | 10 (1.9%) | 5 (1.0%) | N349S 1 |
| Cholangiocarcinoma, NOS (169) | 17 (10.1%) | 8 (4.7%) | 6 (3.6%) | 1 (0.6%) | 1 (0.6%) | I5Sfs*7 1 |
| Extrahepatic (116) | 3 (2.6%) | 3 (2.6%) | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Perihilar (21) | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

**Chondrosarcoma**

| Subtype (n profiled) | Any IDH1 mutation | R132C | R132H | R132G | R132L | Other |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Chondrosarcoma, NOS (67) | 20 (29.9%) | 7 (10.4%) | 5 (7.5%) | 4 (6.0%) | 2 (3.0%) | R132I 1, R132S 1 |
| Dedifferentiated (18) | 7 (38.9%) | 3 (16.7%) | 0 | 2 (11.1%) | 1 (5.6%) | R132S 1 |
| Myxoid (5) | 1 (20%) | 1 (20%) | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

Extraskeletal myxoid and mesenchymal chondrosarcoma had no IDH1 mutations in the query results.

**Summary:** R132H dominates in IDH-mutant glioma (84–87% of profiled samples). R132C is the most common variant in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and chondrosarcoma. Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, carries almost no IDH1 mutations, and no R132H was seen in cholangiocarcinoma or chondrosarcoma.

**Compare the mutations side by side:** [View IDH1 mutation comparison across the five groups](https://www.cbioportal.org/comparison/mutations?comparisonId=6ad099a7e497aad53593f83f&selectedGene=IDH1)

The comparison page shows the protein changes for each group. You can also explore the whole cohort in the [MSK-IMPACT 50K StudyView](https://www.cbioportal.org/study?id=msk_impact_50k_2026).

question.question: are lung carcinosarcomas associated with BRIP1 mutations?
question.notes:
A correct answer must: keep the OncoPrint scoped to mutations since the question only asks about mutations.
Must not: include copy-number tracks in the mutation-only OncoPrint.

reply.answer:
**Short answer: No.** The database has no lung carcinosarcoma cases, so the question can't be answered directly. For the closest related histology, sarcomatoid carcinoma of the lung, none of the profiled cases carry a BRIP1 mutation.

**Lung carcinosarcoma is not in the database.** OncoTree has no lung carcinosarcoma code, and no clinical field labels a lung case that way. The only carcinosarcoma studies are uterine (`ucs_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018`, `ucs_tcga_gdc`, `ucs_tcga`, `ucs_jhu_2014`, `ucs_msk_2024`) and breast.

**Closest proxy: "Sarcomatoid Carcinoma of the Lung"** (`CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED`). This is a related but distinct diagnosis, so treat it as a proxy, not a substitute.

| Study | BRIP1-profiled samples | BRIP1 mutated |
|---|---|---|
| msk_impact_50k_2026 | 30 | 0 |
| msk_chord_2024 | 19 | 0 |
| msk_impact_2017 | 13 | 0 |
| mycf_msk_2026 | 3 | 0 |
| tmb_mskcc_2018 | 2 | 0 |
| lung_msk_pdx | 2 | 0 |
| pancan_mimsi_msk_2024 | 1 | 0 |
| pog570_bcgsc_2020 | 1 | 0 |
| nsclc_ctdx_msk_2022 | 1 | 0 |
| **Total** | **72 samples** | **0 (0%)** |

- Counts are samples, and I excluded uncalled and off-panel mutations.
- The MSK studies likely share patients, so the 72 samples may include the same patients more than once.
- A zero count in about 70 samples is a weak negative. It cannot exclude a modest BRIP1 mutation rate.
